events.text: Noon on the longest day. You are on the ridge above the barley country, and this year, for the first time, you feel the day waiting for you, the way a drum waits for the stick. You open your beak and sing, and the heat goes out of you over the fields in a long wave, and the barley turns from green-gold to gold while the farmers watch. Summer has come because you sang it. The sun hangs there, at the top, listening.

choices.text: Finish the song and let the sun go on down the sky

effects.log: You end on the low note, and the sun tips past the top of the sky and starts down, as it should. The farmers cut the barley the next week, dry and heavy. Summer is yours to start. It was never yours to keep.

choices.text: Hold the last note, and hold the day with it, a little longer

effects.log: You hold the note, and the sun holds with it, white and still, for the length of a meal. Nobody below understands why noon is so long. You do. It is the best you have ever felt. Somewhere in the west, on a cold ridge, something opens its eyes.

choices.text: Sing it low and short, for the farmers, not for the sky

effects.log: A small song, a field song, the kind they sing at the threshing. The barley ripens just as well. A grandmother at the edge of the field looks up, hums the second verse back at you, and goes on cutting.

events.text: Another solstice, and the farmers are waiting for you. They have put a bowl of new barley on a flat stone on the ridge, and a jar of well water beside it, and they stand in the field with their hats off and their faces up. An old farmer at the front says, loud enough for the sky, "Not too long this year. The rice wants rain after the barley, and the rain will not come while the sun is stuck."

choices.text: Sing exactly as long as a summer should be, and no longer

effects.log: You sing it to the length of a breath you did not know you knew. The sun goes over. Three days later the first rain of the monsoon comes up from the south, right on time, and the old farmer stands in it with his hat off.

choices.text: Hold it, just once more. The farmers do not know how good it feels

effects.log: You hold it. The farmers put their hats back on, one by one, and stop looking up. The rain comes eleven days late. The rice is short that year, and the old farmer does not come to the ridge again.

choices.text: Eat the barley and drink the water first, as a guest should

effects.log: You come down to the flat stone and eat every grain and drink the jar, and bow to the field, and then sing. It is the south's way: the guest eats, then the guest sings. The farmers cheer at the bowing more than the singing.

events.text: The solstice again. The day waits for you at noon, as it always does now, white and still and a little too eager. The barley is ripe. The wells are lower than they were.

choices.text: Sing it and let it go

effects.log: You sing, and let go, and the sun goes over. Summer is a thing you start and then give away. You are getting better at the giving.

choices.text: Hold it a little

effects.log: A little longer. The wells go down a hand. The rain comes late. You tell yourself a little is nothing. (The summer you held is counted.)

choices.text: Sing it from the bottom of a cold well instead, so the noon is gentler

effects.log: It is a strange song from the bottom of a well, and the barley ripens a little slower for it, and nobody gets sunstroke in the field. You come up shivering and wet. (-3 health)

events.text: Autumn after autumn the frost has come late and the rice has come in thin, and in the market of the county town they have started to say it out loud: the red bird keeps the summer too long. A swallow brings you the rest of it. On the western ridge, in a cave that faces the setting sun, something white has been seen standing in the mouth, looking east, every evening of this late summer.

choices.text: Promise the swallows, and the sky, that you will let go on time

effects.log: You say it aloud on the ridge-pole at dusk so that it counts. The next solstice you sing and let go on the last note. That autumn the frost comes on the right night, and the white shape in the western cave mouth is not seen again that year.

choices.text: Hold the next one anyway. Summer is yours; let autumn come and take it

effects.log: You hold it longer than ever. The barley stands dry in the field for a week past cutting. In the west, the white shape is in the cave mouth every evening now, and it does not go back in. (The summer you held is counted. Hold it too often and autumn will come for it.)

choices.text: Sing an apology to the rice, field by field, the whole county

effects.log: A song for every field that came in thin, one by one, all autumn. The farmers do not know what the bird is singing to their rice. The rice grows the next year as if it had heard.

events.text: A cold morning at the end of the eighth month. You wake on your ridge with frost on your tail feathers, the first you have ever let settle there, and look west, and the whole western ridge is white and still and patient in a way you do not like. Summer is over. Somebody else's season has come in, and it did not knock.

choices.text: Bow to the west, the way a guest leaves a house

effects.log: You bow to the white ridge. Nothing bows back, but a cold wind comes down off it and lifts your feathers, once, not unkindly. Autumn has its own manners. You are learning them.

choices.text: Think about what a season is, if it does not end

effects.log: A summer that does not end is not a summer. It is a drought with a bird in it. You sit with the frost on your tail until it melts, and you are a little older afterwards.

choices.text: Flare up, and show the west that summer has not gone far

effects.log: You flare red on the ridge at dawn, and every frost for a mile melts at once, and a thatched shed at the foot of the ridge steams and then smokes. The west says nothing. You feel very foolish by noon. (Ash +1)

events.text: The solstice, long years into your life as the Summer Bird. A child in the barley country has made a red paper bird on a stick and runs up the ridge at noon with it, singing a song about you that is mostly wrong, and plants the stick in the ground by the flat stone, and runs down again. The day waits. The paper bird turns in the hot wind.

choices.text: Sing the child's song, wrong words and all

effects.log: The wrong words, the child's tune, sung by the real bird over the whole valley. The child stops halfway down the ridge and turns round with a face like a lamp. Every child in that county sings it your way for generations.

choices.text: Let the paper bird sing it for you: give it your breath for one noon

effects.log: You breathe into the paper bird and it rises off its stick and sings, thin and high, while you sit hidden in the rocks. Summer comes just as well. The child will tell it for the rest of a long life, and nobody will believe it.

choices.text: Hold the day so the child can stay on the ridge a little longer

effects.log: The child stays on the ridge all that long noon, lying on the warm stone, telling the paper bird stories. It is the happiest day the child will have. The rain comes late again. (The summer you held is counted.)

events.text: The first dog day: the third metal day after the solstice. The old people say that in these days metal hides from fire, and they are right. On the western ridge there is a cave that breathes cold, and in its mouth, far back where the sun does not reach, two pale eyes. The White Tiger. It has not come out since the solstice. When your shadow falls across the cave mouth, a deep voice says, "Come back in autumn."

choices.text: "I only came to see if the rumours were true. You hide from a sparrow."

effects.log: "I hide from the season," the voice says, "which happens to be you. In autumn I will come out and you will find another ridge to sit on." There is a pause. "You are smaller than I was told." You are. You find you do not mind.

choices.text: Leave a branch of cold mountain water-cress at the cave mouth, and go

effects.log: You carry it in your beak from a spring three ridges away, cold enough to sting. In the morning it is gone. Nobody thanks you. Nobody growls either.

choices.text: Sit down in the cave mouth and make it a little warmer, for fun

effects.log: You settle in the cave mouth and glow. The cold breath of the cave turns to steam. Far back, the eyes narrow, and a growl comes out that shakes moss off the roof. You leave before the growl finishes, laughing. A pine at the cave mouth is scorched. (Ash +1)

events.text: The middle dog day. In the valleys the people have gone up the streams to cool their feet in the water and sit under the pavilions; the cattle stand in the river to their bellies. You come to the western cave again, because nothing else in the south will argue with you. The voice in the dark asks, without any greeting, "Why is fire so loud? Everything you do, the whole valley hears."

choices.text: "Because a fire nobody hears is a fire nobody feeds."

effects.log: "And a tiger nobody hears," the voice says, "eats." The eyes close. "We are both of us honest, then." You talk until sunset about hunger and fuel. It is the best conversation you have had in a decade.

choices.text: "Why are you so quiet? Everything you do, nobody hears until it is too late."

effects.log: A long silence. Then something like a laugh, from very deep in the cave. "Come back in autumn," it says, "and ask me that on my ridge." It is, you realise, an invitation.

choices.text: Bring it ice from the state ice house, the officials' ration, in your claws

effects.log: One block from the river ice house, stamped for a minister. It melts half away on the flight and burns your claws with cold the whole way. You drop what is left in the cave mouth. The eyes look at it, and at you, for a long time. "Fire," says the voice, "carrying ice." (-6 health)

events.text: The last dog day, and the voice in the cave is bored, and a bored tiger is a cruel one. "They say in the south," it says, "that you burned a magistrate's beard over a word. That you cannot sit through a festival without setting a hat on fire. That your temper is the only thing about you that is bigger than a sparrow."

choices.text: Swallow it, and wish the tiger a cool autumn

effects.log: You swallow it. It goes down hot and sits under your breastbone with the others. "A cool autumn to you," you say, very politely, and fly off. Behind you, the cave is quiet for a long time.

choices.text: Sing it: a song about a tiger afraid of a sparrow

effects.log: You sing it from a pine across the gorge, every verse sillier than the last. The valley people cooling their feet in the stream below laugh until they fall in. From the cave, at the end, one low sound, which might be a growl and might be the chorus.

choices.text: Let it out: flare at the cave until the moss on the roof catches

effects.log: The moss catches, and the dry grass at the cave mouth, and for a moment the whole face of the ridge smokes. Deep inside, the tiger is laughing at you, a slow heavy laugh. You have proved its point exactly. (Ash +1)

events.text: First frost. You fly west at dawn, as you were told, and the western ridge is not a ridge with a cave in it any more. It is the White Tiger's, every stone of it, white and sharp and awake, and the cold comes off it like a held breath. Somewhere on it, unseen, a voice says, "Now ask me why I am quiet."

choices.text: Ask it, and listen to the whole answer

effects.log: It talks about judging. About how the guilty hear nothing until the end, and why that is mercy, and why it is not. You listen with your feathers held tight against the cold. When it finishes, the sun is up and you are both quiet.

choices.text: Answer your own question first: why fire must be loud

effects.log: You tell it about the fire jar on the coldest night, and a child blowing on a spark. A fire has to be heard to be kept. The ridge listens without a sound. "Then be loud," it says at last, "in summer."

choices.text: Bow on the edge of its ridge, and go home before you are asked to

effects.log: You bow, on the very edge, where its stone begins, and turn for the south. Behind you the cold eases a little. The south says the red bird and the white tiger are enemies. The south has never seen them in the right season.

events.text: The dog days again. The valley people are in the streams; the dogs are flat in the shade; the cave on the western ridge is breathing cold, and the pale eyes are in it.

choices.text: Go and talk through the cave mouth

effects.log: An afternoon of talk across the line where the heat stops. Neither of you crosses it. That is the friendship: a line, and two voices.

choices.text: Leave it be. Metal hides from fire for good reason

effects.log: You keep to the eastern side of every ridge all season, so your heat does not reach its cave. In autumn, a swallow brings word: the tiger noticed.

choices.text: Cool a village instead: sit high and still and draw the heat off the roofs

effects.log: You sit on the highest roof and pull the heat of the village into yourself all afternoon, until you are red to the tail and the old people in the shade stop fanning. A fire can take heat as well as give it. It hurts. (-3 health)

events.text: A fire of yours has grown fierce, and a swallow brings word from an unexpected direction: the White Tiger has sent a message, by a magpie, which is the only bird it trusts. The magpie is very nervous about delivering it to you. "The western wind owes the south a favour," it recites. "One cold night, wherever you want it."

choices.text: Take the cold night: lay it over the fierce fire and calm the sickness round it

effects.log: One night the wind comes off the western ridge out of season, cold and clean, and settles over the house where your old fire burns too hot. The fevers break by morning. You do not see the tiger. You are very sure it saw you.

choices.text: Thank it, and say you will renew your own fires

effects.log: "Tell it a fire should be kept by the one who lit it," you tell the magpie. The magpie repeats it word for word to the west, and the west, the magpie reports, made a sound that might have been approval.

events.text: A clear summer night, and you learn from an old astronomer muttering on a palace roof that the bright red star low in the east, the one that rises as summer begins, is called the Great Fire. It is the heart of the Azure Dragon's mansions. You look at it a long time. A star called the Great Fire, that rises when summer begins, sitting in the east, in a dragon's chest.

choices.text: It belongs in the south. Fly east and ask for it

effects.log: You go east that night, over three ranges, toward the long ridge where the storms sleep. It is the most presumptuous thing you have ever done. You enjoy every mile.

choices.text: Leave it where it is. A heart is not a thing you borrow

effects.log: You sit with the astronomer until the star sets. You decide, in the end, that a fire in someone else's chest is theirs. The astronomer never knows a bird thought about it.

choices.text: Sing to it from the southern hills, so it knows it has a cousin

effects.log: All night, a song to a star. Near dawn the Great Fire flickers, once, red and low. Probably the air. Probably.

events.text: The eastern ridge. You know it is the Azure Dragon's from a valley away: the pines on it lie like scales, the streams run down its flanks like whiskers, and a storm is asleep along its spine. You land on a rock at its foot and the whole ridge goes still in the way a great creature goes still when it is listening. You say what you have come for. The thunder answers before the voice does.

choices.text: Ask humbly: for one night, to light the south's summer

ok.log: A long silence. Then: "One night. You are younger than I was when I learned what a heart costs." The storm along the ridge parts like a curtain, and something red and enormous comes loose from the east and sets down, burning, in the south. One night.

fail.log: "No," the ridge says, without heat. "Come back when you know why not." The storm turns over in its sleep. You fly home with nothing, and spend a decade working out why not.

choices.text: Offer a trade: your fire for the rain-keepers of its valley in winter

effects.log: "Trade," says the ridge, sounding almost amused. "The south does love a banquet." Every winter after, the dragon's rain-shrine keepers find their stoves burning on the coldest mornings. And one summer night the Great Fire comes south.

choices.text: Demand it. Fire belongs to the south

effects.log: You say it, and the ridge does not answer, and so you say it louder, and a stand of pines on the dragon's flank catches from the heat of your saying it. A cold rain comes down on you out of a clear sky and puts out the pines and you, both. You fly home steaming. (Ash +1)

events.text: The night of the loan. The Great Fire sits low over the southern sea, enormous and red, and every fire of yours on the earth answers it: the hearths flare, the beacons stand up straight, the lantern on the ferry burns like a second moon. You have never been this strong. Dawn is coming. The dragon said one night.

choices.text: Give it back as the sky greys, exactly on time

effects.log: You carry it east yourself, at the end of the night, in front of you like a lantern too big to hold. The ridge takes it back without a word. Weeks later, a rain falls on a dry county of yours that you never asked for.

choices.text: Keep it one hour past dawn, to warm a fishing fleet out at sea

effects.log: One hour. A fleet comes home through a cold fog by its light. Then you take it east, late, and the ridge says nothing at all, and the silence is worse than thunder. (The summer you held is counted.)

choices.text: Use it to renew every fire you have, all at once, before you give it back

ok.log: One sweep of the south with the Great Fire held in front of you, and every fire you keep is rubbed new at once. You get it back to the east as the sun clears the sea. The ridge notices exactly how close it was.

fail.log: It is too big. It slips, and a hillside of dry grass under it goes up, and you spend the last of the night beating the fire out with your own wings. You return the star late and singed. (Ash +1, -10 health)

events.text: Decades after you went east. A summer storm comes down on the south out of a clear sky, and in the middle of it, on the wind, a single cold drop lands on your crest and does not hiss. It is a message. The eastern ridge has remembered you, one way or the other.

choices.text: Answer with one warm wind east, to dry its rain-keepers' washing

effects.log: One warm wind, on the right day. In the east, a line of washing dries in an hour, and a whole village of rain-keepers thinks it is lucky. The ridge knows exactly who it was.

choices.text: Fly east and bow at the foot of the ridge, the whole way down

effects.log: A long flight to bow once. The ridge says nothing, as dragons do, but that summer it rains on your driest county for three days, gently, and you know. (-4 health)

choices.text: Ignore it. The east has its sky and the south has its own

effects.log: You let the drop dry on your crest. The east does not send another. You tell yourself that is how you wanted it.

events.text: North of the river, a new capital: walls going up, a palace laid out by geomancers with strings and compasses, facing south as palaces must. And due south of it, across the river, a mountain of bare rock with a summit that goes up in sharp tongues, exactly like a fire. You land on the topmost tongue. It is warm already. It fits you. Every palace roof in the capital is looking straight at you.

choices.text: Stay. Sit on the summit every evening and look at the city

effects.log: Every evening, a red bird on the flame-shaped peak. In the palace, the geomancers begin to have meetings. You do not hear them. You can guess.

choices.text: Sit there one evening, then go. It is too pointed a thing to do

effects.log: One evening is enough to see the whole court come out on the terraces and stare south. You leave before dark. The mountain stays the shape it is. They will worry about it anyway.

choices.text: Stay, and keep perfectly cool, so the city learns a fire can sit still

effects.log: You sit on the summit with your fire banked so low it hurts, every evening for a year. The city does not trust it. Cities never trust a quiet fire. (-3 health)

events.text: The geomancers have reported. The mountain to the south is a fire mountain, and the bird on it is fire upon fire, and the new capital burns too easily. Before the southern gate a gang of labourers is digging a square pond, and the court astrologer stands on the bank telling them where to put the water so it lies between the palace and your peak. A pond against a bird.

choices.text: Watch from the peak, and admire the pond. It is a good pond

effects.log: It is a very good pond, square and deep, with lotus in it by the next summer. You come down one night and drink from it, which causes a crisis at court. The astrologer insists the bird drinking proves the pond works.

choices.text: Ask the swallows what the city says of you

effects.log: The swallows under the new eaves report: the city is afraid of fire, all fire, and you are the shape it gives its fear. Every thatched quarter that burns this year is your doing, says the market. None of them is.

choices.text: Dry the pond with one hot noon, to show what a pond is worth

effects.log: One afternoon and the pond is a square of cracked mud with frogs in it. The labourers refill it with buckets for a week. The court adds a second pond. You have made the city twice as afraid of you, and gained nothing. (Ash +1)

events.text: The great southern gate is finished, and its name-board goes up: the Gate of Exalted Rites. Every other gate in the wall has its name written across. This one has it written down, from top to bottom, so that the characters stand up like a flame. A scholar on the gate explains it to the crowd: fire against fire. The board faces your peak.

choices.text: Bow to the gate. Rites are your virtue; it bears your virtue's name

effects.log: You come down to the gate at dawn and bow to the name-board, low, the way the south bows. The gate guards drop their spears. The name was meant to hold you off. It is courtesy, and courtesy is yours. You find that you are proud of the city.

choices.text: Swallow it. A whole city arming against you, and you have burned nothing

effects.log: Nothing. Not one roof. And a gate-name hung on end against you, and a pond, and the whole court praying. You swallow it, and it is the biggest coal you have ever swallowed.

choices.text: Laugh. It is the best joke the city has made

effects.log: You laugh on the peak so hard you shed a feather, and the feather drifts across the river burning, and lands on the gate roof, and goes out on the tiles. Nobody is hurt. The city is sure it was an attack. (Ash +1)

events.text: At the palace gate two stone beasts are set up, facing south, facing your peak: squat, maned, with a single horn and a look of great patience. The masons say they eat fire. The court says so too. One night you fly over the palace wall to see them close, and the left-hand one's stone eyes seem to follow you across the sky.

choices.text: Land in front of it and look it in the eye

effects.log: You stand in front of a stone beast in the moonlight for an hour, face to face. It does not move. You are almost sure it does not move. When you leave, the stone where you stood is cold, as if something had drunk the heat out of it.

choices.text: Leave them be. A thing set to guard against you deserves respect

effects.log: You never fly over that gate again. The court decides the stone beasts work. Perhaps they do. You know you chose.

events.text: A fire in the palace kitchens on a windy night: a cook's lamp, a rack of dried peppers, the eaves. Not yours. But every face on the palace wall turns south to your peak, and by morning the court has decided. A rite is ordered to drive the fire bird off the mountain: drums, red-bean porridge flung at the south, a decree read aloud to the rock.

choices.text: Fly into the palace, call the kitchen fire home into your breast, and leave

ok.log: You come down out of the dark into the smoke and the fire comes to you like a dog to a whistle, and you are gone before the guards can see more than a red rush over the wall. The court is more afraid than ever. The cooks, who saw, are not.

fail.log: It is not your fire, and it does not know your call. You get half of it before it gets you, and leave the rest to the bucket lines, and fly home scorched with the whole palace shouting that the bird came to finish the job. (-14 health)

choices.text: Let them blame you. Sit on the peak through the drums and the porridge

effects.log: The drums go on for three days. The porridge falls short of the river. You sit through all of it, very still, and the fire you did not light goes into your record anyway, in the city's.

choices.text: Burn the gate's name-board, once, so they know what a real fire of yours looks like

effects.log: One pass in the dark. The vertical name-board of the southern gate burns from top to bottom like a candle and is gone. The city wails. In the morning they carve a new one and hang it, on end, again. You feel nothing like as good as you expected. (Ash +2)

events.text: Decades on the fire mountain. The pond has lotus in it, the gate has its name on end, and the city has grown up afraid of you and a little proud of you, the way a village is of a dangerous river. This evening you feel the peak under your claws differently. You could stay. Not as a bird on a mountain: as the mountain's fire, for good, and the city facing you for as long as there is a city.

choices.text: Make peace: fly down to the pond, drink, bow to the gate, and leave the mountain

effects.log: You drink from the pond at dawn, bow to the name-board, and fly south over the river and do not come back. The city keeps its pond and its gate and its stone beasts for five hundred years, against a bird that is no longer there. You think they like having them.

choices.text: Stay a bird. Sit on the peak some evenings, and other evenings not

effects.log: You keep the mountain the way you keep everything: you come and you go. The city never knows which evenings to fear. You think that is probably healthy for a city.

choices.text: Become the mountain. Guardian and danger at once, for as long as the city stands

effects.log: You fold your wings on the highest tongue of rock and let go of being a bird. In the morning the peak is warm to the touch, always, and the court geomancers write that the fire of the south mountain is very strong this reign, and dig the pond a little deeper.

events.text: A spring noon with a northwest wind, the kind that lifts straw off roofs. In the capital, in a servant's house south of the market, somebody knocks over a brazier. By the time you see the smoke from your ridge it is not a fire any more but a running thing, going south and east across the thatch faster than a horse. Two thousand roofs lie in its path. It is not yours. You did not give it. It does not know your name.
events.arc: The Great Fire of the Capital

choices.text: Fly into it and try to call it home, a fire that is not yours

ok.log: It does not know you, and it does not want to come. You call it anyway, roof by roof, the way you would call a frightened dog, and some of it comes, into your breast, burning. You hold a whole street of fire in you until the bucket lines reach it. (-10 health)

fail.log: It will not come. You are fire, and it is fire, and it simply eats you a little, the way it is eating everything. You fall out of the smoke onto a well-head and lie there while the city burns past you. (-18 health)

choices.text: Fly to your own keepers in the city first, and get them out

effects.log: A clerk who keeps a lamp of yours, a grandmother whose kitchen fire is your hearth's cousin: you go to them first, and lead them north against the wind, and then go back for their neighbours, and then theirs. You do not save the city. You save a street.

choices.text: Go high and lead people out by your light, away from the wind

effects.log: Above the smoke, burning bright as a lamp in the noon, you turn and turn over the safe streets until the crowds see you and follow. They run toward the bird of fire, away from the fire. Nobody will ever be able to explain that to a magistrate.

events.text: The second day. The fire is out, and then in the afternoon the wind gets up again and it comes back to life in the ash of the first, and jumps the wall of a royal villa, and runs. The king is away hunting. The watchtower bell has been ringing so long the ringer's hands are bleeding.
events.arc: The Great Fire of the Capital

choices.text: Take the bell rope from the ringer and ring the whole city awake

effects.log: You hang on the rope with your claws and swing, and the great bell rings out over the burning city in a rhythm no human could keep. Every house in the north half turns out with water. The ringer sits at the foot of the tower and cries.

choices.text: Fight the wind itself: fly against it with everything you have

ok.log: You hang in the northwest wind with your wings spread, hot against cold, and for an hour the wind bends round you and the fire has nothing to ride. The bucket lines catch it. You come down so tired you cannot lift your head. (-8 health)

fail.log: The wind takes you like a leaf and throws you across the river. When you get back the villa is gone. (-15 health)

choices.text: Carry children out of the villa's servants' quarter, one at a time

effects.log: Eleven trips through the smoke, a child in your claws each time, burning your feathers to the quill. Eleven children. On the twelfth trip there is nobody left to carry. (-12 health)

events.text: After the fire, an office. The court founds a fire office under the Board of War, with men to watch from the towers and laws about firewalls and tiles and how close a house may stand to its neighbour. And a file. A clerk of the new office has been told to find the causes of the great fire, and every witness the clerk asks has the same thing to say: there was a red bird in it.
events.arc: The Great Fire of the Capital

choices.text: Perch on the fire office roof and let them write what they like

effects.log: The file grows for years: a red bird at every fire in the south, cause or cure unknown. You sit on its roof some evenings while they write it. A fire office with a red bird on its roof is a joke the whole capital enjoys.

choices.text: Leave it. Every fire is somebody's business; let it be theirs

effects.log: The fire office builds its walls and lays its tiles and stations its watchmen, and the city burns less, a little less every year. You did not do it. You find you are glad you did not.

choices.text: Burn the file. It is wrong, and it is about you

effects.log: One night, one window, and the file is ash on the desk. The clerk opens a new file the next morning, titled with a single line about a red bird burning a file about a red bird. (Ash +1)

events.text: On the ridge-pole of the new fire office, at dusk. Below in the yard {npc}, the clerk who keeps the file on you, is eating rice alone from a box on the steps. {He} looks up, and sees you, and does not run. "I have a question for the file," {he} says, chopsticks in the air. "Are you the cause of fire, or the cure for it?"
events.arc: The Great Fire of the Capital

choices.text: "Both. Write both. A fire office that forgets it should be closed"

mem.note: answered my file

effects.log: {npc} writes it down on the step, in {his} good hand, with the rice going cold. Both. The fire office keeps that page at the front of the file for two hundred years. New clerks are made to read it on the first day.

choices.text: Teach {him} how a fire is born: a brazier, a wind, a roof of straw

mem.note: taught me how fires begin

effects.log: You talk until the stars are out: wind, fuel, a gap between houses, the way a roof breathes. {npc} fills twelve pages and then a thirteenth. The next year the fire office makes a law about braziers on windy days, and it is a good one.

choices.text: "Ask the fire." Then flare once and go

effects.log: You flare on the ridge-pole and the clerk's rice box catches. {npc} beats it out with the file. When you look back {he} is laughing, alone in the yard, holding a singed page. (Ash +1)

mem.note: burned my supper and I laughed

events.text: Decades after the great fire. The capital has walls of brick between its quarters now, and broad roads that a fire cannot jump, and tile where there was thatch, and a watchman in every tower who rings the bell at the first thread of smoke. It burns less. It still burns. The fire office has a red bird painted on its gate, nobody alive remembers why.
events.arc: The Great Fire of the Capital

choices.text: Sit on the painted gate one evening, as if you were the picture

effects.log: A watchman coming off duty sees the painted bird on the gate and the real one sitting on top of it, and stops, and looks from one to the other for a long time, and goes home without saying anything to anyone.

choices.text: Fly the city's firewalls end to end, and warm every watchtower one cold night

effects.log: Every tower, every watchman, one warm night in the hardest week of winter. They stay awake for it. That spring a fire in the leather market is caught before the second roof.

choices.text: Think about it: a city learned to keep its fires. Without you

effects.log: Walls, roads, tiles, bells. Not one of them a bird. It is the best thing you have seen a city do, and you had nothing to do with it, except perhaps that you were what it was afraid of.

events.text: A village in the hills with a fever in it, the kind that goes house to house and does not leave. The headman has hung a red talisman on the gate, written in cheap ink, and it has faded in the rain to pink. Your crest has been burning for a year now. You could pull one feather of your own fire and write on the world with it. You have never tried. A feather is a piece of you.

choices.text: Pull the feather and write the talisman over the gate

effects.log: It hurts like pulling out a tooth. The feather writes on the yellow paper in red that glows in the dark, and the fever stops at the gate like a dog at a threshold. The headman frames the talisman. Somebody from the medicine market is already asking where the ink came from. (-5 health)

choices.text: Write it on the headman's palm instead, where nobody can sell it

effects.log: Red on a palm, warm as a coal. The headman walks house to house with it for a month and lays the hand on every sick forehead. The fever goes. The mark fades with it. Nobody can grind a palm into ink. (-5 health)

choices.text: Do not. A bird that writes on the world will be asked to write everything

effects.log: You sit on the gate all night instead, keeping the sick houses warm. Some of them live who would not have. Some do not. You keep the feather. You are not sure, afterwards, that you were right.

events.text: A decree is posted in the county town: every household to send one man to the magistrate's new walls for the whole of the planting season. If the men go, the rice is not planted. If it is not planted, there is no rice. The magistrate wrote it himself, in a fine hand. It is pasted to the board in the market, and the market stands in front of it in silence.

choices.text: Correct it in vermilion, overnight: "after the harvest"

ok.log: Three words, in a red that will not wash off, in a hand so like the magistrate's that the magistrate himself is not sure he did not write them. The men plant the rice. The walls go up in the autumn. Nobody is flogged, because nobody can prove anything. (-5 health)

fail.log: Your correction is right and your hand is wrong: plainly, gloriously red, plainly not his. The magistrate has the board burned and the decree reposted, and puts a guard on it, and a reward on the bird. The market remembers both boards. (-5 health)

choices.text: Leave the decree. Perch on the magistrate's roof and talk him out of it

effects.log: It takes three nights of a red bird on his ridge-pole, saying the same sensible thing about rice. On the fourth morning a new notice goes up: the men will come after the harvest, by order, in the magistrate's fine hand.

choices.text: Write it in fire across the magistrate's own door instead

effects.log: The words burn into the door of the magistrate's house overnight, a hand high: THE RICE FIRST. The door smokes for a week. The decree is withdrawn. The magistrate never sleeps well again, and you have written in anger. (Ash +1)

events.text: The county's register of bonded servants is kept in a lacquered box in the office of records: names, owners, the price, the children's names written in as they are born. A girl of fourteen is sweeping the office floor. Her name is in the box. So are her mother's and her grandmother's. You are on the window ledge, and your crest is burning, and the box is not locked.

choices.text: Burn one name: hers, and her mother's, and her grandmother's

effects.log: Three names, three lines, gone as if they had never been written, and the ink will not take on that paper again. The girl sweeps on and does not know. It will take the county a year to notice, and by then the family has walked south and is someone else. (-5 health)

choices.text: Leave it. Teach the girl to read the box instead, from the window, one night a week

effects.log: It takes two winters. She learns her letters off the register itself, and then the law, and at twenty-two she goes to the magistrate with a petition in her own hand about a clause her grandmother was bought under. It is a long road. It is hers.

choices.text: Burn the whole register, box and all

effects.log: One breath. The lacquer box goes up like a torch, and the shelves behind it, and half the office of records. Two hundred families are free by morning, and the office is ash, and the girl with the broom is outside, alive, staring. A great good, done in fire. (Ash +2)

events.text: A provincial governor has heard of the red bird that writes. He has a feather of yours in a jar, a moulted one, and a scholar with a pen, and a list: talismans for his granary, his sons, his storehouse, his enemies' doors. He reads the list aloud on his veranda, to the sky, expecting you to be listening. You are. The last line is "and something for the magistrate who crossed me".

choices.text: Swallow it. Fly away and let the jar stay a jar

effects.log: The list goes on in your head for days. Granary, sons, enemies. You keep it, hot, with everything else you keep.

choices.text: Sing it: the whole list, set to a tune, from his own ridge-pole

effects.log: Every item, in order, to the tune of a children's counting rhyme. By market day the province is singing his list back to him. He leaves the feather in its jar and the jar in a cupboard and never mentions you again.

choices.text: Write him one talisman, in the sky over his house: GREED

effects.log: One word, in fire, a whole night long, hanging over his roof where the province can see it. He never asks again. His granary is opened by his own frightened steward that winter. You wrote in anger. (Ash +1)

events.text: The medicine markets have done their sums: the bird that writes talismans writes them with its own feathers, and a feather of yours is worth a village. The nets are out again on every ridge-pole in the south: fine silk nets, soaked so they will not burn, and men under them with long poles and patient faces.

choices.text: Fly the summer wind for a season and let them forget you

effects.log: A season on the hot wind over the southern sea. The nets hang empty on the ridge-poles until they rot. The men go home and tell their children about the bird that never came.

choices.text: Burn a net in front of the netters, slowly, so they see it is pointless

ok.log: The wet silk hisses and steams and then, very slowly, browns, while six netters watch with their mouths open. They roll up the rest of the nets and walk home. Word goes round the markets: the bird can burn wet silk.

fail.log: While you are burning the first net the second comes down over you from behind. It takes all your heat and half your feathers to get out of it. (-12 health)

choices.text: Moult somewhere they will find the feathers, and let them have those

effects.log: A moult in a cold kiln on purpose, the old feathers left in a heap. The netters find them and sell them, and the talismans written with them are good, and warm a hundred houses. Moulted fire is still fire. It cost you nothing to give.

events.text: It starts as an itch on the top of your head, and then a heat, and then one morning on the ridge-pole you shake yourself and a crest stands up on your head that is not feathers. It is flame: living, steady, the colour of the heart of a kiln. The roof tiles under you are warm through. A magistrate's clerk crossing the yard below drops an armful of scrolls.

choices.text: Look at your reflection in the yard's rain barrel for a long time

effects.log: A red bird with a crown of fire looks back at you out of the barrel, and the water steams around it. You look until the clerk has picked up all the scrolls. You are not a sparrow. You never quite believed it until now.

choices.text: Try to bank it low, the way a good fire jar is banked

effects.log: It takes a month to learn to bank a crest. When you have, it burns a hand high and no higher, unless you are angry. You learn, also, that you will always know when you are angry now, because your crest will tell you.

events.text: Some time with the crest, and the world has noticed. Officials bow when you pass over a county seat. Children point. Grandmothers bring their sick grandchildren out into the yard to stand under your shadow. And a magistrate in the next county has sent a polite letter to the sky, pinned to his gate, asking the Flame-Crested Bird to adjudicate a dispute between two villages over a well.

choices.text: Adjudicate it: the well is for whoever is thirstiest this year

effects.log: You sit on the well-head all summer and watch, and give the water to the village with the sick children, and next summer to the other. Both villages hate the ruling. Both drink. That is a judgment.

choices.text: Decline politely: you change the world, you do not run it

effects.log: You burn the word NO very small and very neatly into the corner of his letter and pin it back on his gate. The magistrate has it framed. The villages settle it themselves, eventually, with a second well.

choices.text: Let the crest flare at the honour of it

effects.log: Your crest goes up a yard high at the thought, and the magistrate's letter on the gate catches, and his gate-roof smokes. He takes it as an answer. Nobody knows what the answer was. (Ash +1)

events.text: The armies of the five directions march under five colours, and the southern army's is red. This year a new general of the south has had a new banner made for it: red silk, and on the red, in gold and vermilion, a bird with a tail like a whirlwind of flame. You. The banner goes past under your ridge on the coast road, with two thousand men behind it. They are marching to the sea, where there are sails.
events.arc: The Red Banner of the South

choices.text: Fly above the banner, the whole march, so the men can see

effects.log: Two thousand men look up from the road and see the bird on their banner and the bird over it, and the march turns into something else: a song, then a run. The general rides under you without once looking up. The general knew you would come.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge. An army is not a fire you gave

effects.log: You watch the red go by and do not follow. War is a fire that someone else lit. You are not sure whether that makes it none of your business, or entirely your business.

choices.text: Follow at a distance, to see what they do with your colour

effects.log: You keep a ridge behind them all the way to the coast. They march well. They do not burn villages. They sing badly. You decide, for now, that they can keep the colour.

events.text: The night before the landing. You are on the ridge-pole of the fishing headman's house where the general has made camp, and {npc} comes out alone into the yard in a plain coat, looks straight up at you, and speaks as if you had been talking for an hour already. "The sails are raiders, four hundred of them, and they will land at dawn on the beach below. Fight beside us. Or tell me why not."
events.arc: The Red Banner of the South

choices.text: "I will fly in front of your banner. I will not burn men on a beach"

mem.note: would fly for us but would not burn

effects.log: {npc} nods as if that were the answer {he} wanted. "Then fly where they can see you," {he} says, "and I will do the rest." {He} goes in. You do not sleep.

choices.text: "I will fight. The coast is mine to keep"

mem.note: swore to fight beside us

effects.log: {npc} bows, low, the south's bow. "Then the coast is lucky," {he} says, "and the raiders are not." You sit on the ridge-pole all night with your crest burning, waiting for the light.

choices.text: "Why should a fire choose between two fleets of men?"

mem.note: asked why it should choose

effects.log: "Because one of them is burning your villages," {npc} says, "and the other is standing in them." {He} waits. You do not answer. In the morning the banner goes down the beach without you, and you watch from the cliff.

events.text: Dawn on the beach. The raiders come through the surf in a grey wave with their boats behind them, and the red banner goes down the dunes to meet them, and {npc} under it. In the middle of the raiders' line a tall captain in lacquered armour is cutting a road toward the banner, and the soldiers round {npc} are falling back from {him}.
events.arc: The Red Banner of the South

choices.text: Drop on the raiders' captain out of the sun

ok.log: Out of the sunrise like a coal from a kiln. The captain's lacquer smokes and blisters and the captain goes down on the sand, alive, disarmed, staring up. The raiders' line breaks at the place where their captain was. {npc} does not look up. {He} only raises the banner higher.

fail.deathCause: a raider captain's spear on a beach, under a red banner
fail.log: The captain is ready for you. A spear-butt takes you out of the air into the surf, and the sea puts out half your fire before you can drag yourself up the beach. The line holds anyway, barely. (-25 health)

choices.text: Fly above the banner, bright as a second sun, and let the army do it

effects.log: You hang over the banner burning, all morning, and the army fights under you as if you were holding it up. The raiders look at you more than at the spears in front of them. By noon they are back in their boats.

choices.text: Burn the beached boats behind them, so they have to surrender, not die

effects.log: Every boat on the sand goes up behind them, one long line of fire. The raiders turn round, see it, and throw down their weapons in the surf. Four hundred men alive who would have fought to the last. You burned their boats. It is still Ash. (Ash +1)

events.text: The victory feast at the county seat. A minister has come down from the capital with the king's thanks, and wants the banner. The bird on it, says the minister, brought victory; the banner should go to the capital and hang in the ancestral shrine of the royal house, where it can be seen to belong to the throne. {npc} is standing very still.
events.arc: The Red Banner of the South

choices.text: Settle on the banner's pole in front of the whole feast

effects.log: You come down out of the night onto the top of the banner pole, crest burning. Nobody at the feast says anything about the capital for the rest of the evening. The banner stays with {npc}, and with the south.

choices.text: Let the banner go. A picture of you is only a picture

effects.log: The banner goes north in a lacquered box. It hangs in a royal shrine for generations, getting dustier. {npc} has a new one made, plainer, and it is the one the south loves.

choices.text: Laugh at the minister until the gauze hat smokes

effects.log: Your laugh comes down the chimney into the feast hall and the minister's gauze hat begins, gently, to smoke. The hall roars. The minister leaves without the banner, and without much of the hat. (Ash +1)

events.text: {npc} is old, and a red banner is folded on a chest at the end of the bed in a house on the coast. The sea is loud tonight. You are in the window. {He} has had the shutters opened so {he} can see the water.
events.arc: The Red Banner of the South

choices.text: Burn soft in the window all night, like the banner did at dawn

effects.npcPass: old age, by an open window over the sea, a red banner folded at the foot of the bed
effects.log: "You came," {npc} says, and then nothing else for a long time. Near dawn {he} asks you to tell the banner it can rest. You tell it. The family buries {npc} with the banner over the coffin, red on the south side of the grave.

choices.text: Tell {him} about every village on the coast that is still standing

effects.npcPass: old age, listening to the names of villages
effects.log: You name them, one by one, north to south along the coast, every one the raiders did not burn. {npc} falls asleep somewhere in the middle, and you finish the list anyway, all the way to the last fishing hamlet, so it is said.

events.text: A strait between an island and the cliffs of the coast, where the tide runs like a river. An admiral, {npc}, has sent a boy up the cliff with a message for the red bird: the enemy fleet is anchored in the strait, two hundred ships, and the tide turns at midnight. {npc} has thirty small boats packed with straw and pine resin. {He} wants to know if a fire set on the tide will keep burning when it reaches them.

choices.text: "It will burn. I will ride the first boat and make sure"

mem.note: promised to ride the fire-boats

effects.log: The boy runs down the cliff with your answer before you have finished it. At the turn of the tide you are sitting in the bow of the first fire-boat, glowing, with twenty-nine more strung out behind you in the dark.

choices.text: "Ask me which ships, not whether"

mem.note: asked which ships

effects.log: The boy comes back up the cliff an hour later, out of breath. "The admiral says: the warships. Not the ones with the rowers chained in them." It is the right answer. You go down to the boats.

choices.text: "Fire on the water is fire nobody can call home. Find another way"

mem.note: would not lend your fire to the strait

effects.log: {npc} reads your answer on the beach and folds it into {his} sleeve. The fire-boats go out at midnight without you. Half of them drift onto the island and burn there, uselessly, all night. The other half are enough.

events.text: Midnight, and the tide turns, and the fire-boats go. You are in the bow of the first, and the strait runs under you like a horse. Ahead, two hundred dark hulls at anchor. Among them, low in the water, a dozen long galleys with oars out, and from them, on the wind, the clank of chains: rowers, prisoners taken from the coast villages, chained to their benches.

choices.text: Steer the fire to the warships, and away from the galleys

ok.log: Boat by boat you lean the fire on the current, and the current obeys, and the fire goes where you point it: the tall warships burn, and the galleys swing on their anchors untouched in the red light. By dawn the rowers are being cut out of their chains by fishermen in skiffs.

fail.log: The tide is stronger than you. Most of the fire goes where you point it. Two boats do not, and two galleys burn with the warships. You do not stay to hear it. You will hear it later anyway. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Go ahead of the fire and break the galleys' chains first

effects.log: You go through the galleys one by one, burning through iron, while the fire-boats wait on the tide behind you as long as they can. The rowers go over the side and swim. Then the fire comes. (-15 health)

choices.text: Burn everything in the strait. A fleet is a fleet

effects.log: Every ship in the strait burns, the warships and the galleys, the masts going down one after another into the red water. The coast is saved. The rowers were from the coast. Nobody on the coast ever sings about that night. (Ash +5)

events.text: The morning after. The strait is full of black timber turning slowly on the tide. Men are clinging to it: enemy sailors, burned, half drowned, calling out in a language the fishermen do not speak. The fishermen on the cliff are watching. Some of them have boat-hooks. They are waiting to see what the red bird does.

choices.text: Fly low over the water and lead the fishing skiffs out to pull them in

effects.log: You go out over the water slowly, from one clinging man to the next, and the skiffs follow your light. Forty men are pulled out alive. The coast puts them to work mending the walls they came to burn. Most of them never go home, and some of them marry into the coast.

choices.text: Leave it to the fishermen. It is their coast

effects.log: You fly back to the ridge. What happens in the strait that morning is not your fire. You do not ask about it afterwards, and nobody tells you.

choices.text: Warm the water where they are, so they last until the tide brings them in

effects.log: Hours over the cold strait, hot as an oven, so the sea round the wreckage stays warm as a bath. The tide brings them in, living, to a beach full of fishermen with boat-hooks, who look at the bird and put them down. (-6 health)

events.text: Years later, on the cliff over the strait, a shrine: a little stone house for the souls of the drowned, both fleets, with rice set out for them on the first and fifteenth of the month. The fishermen built it. Somebody has painted a red bird on its lintel, small, in the corner, not looking at anyone.

choices.text: Light the shrine's lamp every night of the summer

effects.log: The shrine lamp is never out that summer. The fishermen say the drowned are keeping it. You let them say it. It is more or less true.

choices.text: Sit on the lintel beside the painted bird for one night, and remember

effects.log: All the ships, all the faces in the red water, all night. In the morning the fisherman who comes with the rice sees two red birds on the lintel, one painted and one not, and bows to both.

events.text: You have flown over the palace of the capital a hundred times. Tonight, for the first time, you feel watched from the ground. At the gate the stone fire-eater sits on its plinth facing south, the way it always has, horn and mane and patient stone mouth. Except that its head is turned a little, now, toward you. You are sure it was not, at dusk.
events.arc: The Stone at the Palace Gate

choices.text: Land on the gate roof and stare back all night

effects.log: All night. It does not blink, because it is stone. You do not blink, because you are proud. At dawn the gate guards change, and when you look again the stone head faces due south, as it always has. You do not believe it for a moment.

choices.text: Fly on. Whatever it is, it is doing its work

effects.log: You fly on south. Behind you, at the gate, a stone head turns back toward the mountain, slowly, the way a guard turns back to the road when a traveller has passed.

events.text: A summer night, very hot, and the stone fire-eater at the palace gate is warm to the touch from the day's sun. You come down to the plinth. It is not entirely stone. There is something under the stone that is awake and judging, the way a magistrate is awake behind a screen. It does not speak. It does not need to. You know what it is measuring: whether you have come to harm the house it guards.
events.arc: The Stone at the Palace Gate

choices.text: Bow to it, the full southern bow, and let it measure

effects.log: You bow, low, wings folded, crest banked to an ember. A long, long moment. Then the warmth goes out of the stone, as if something had decided you could be let alone, and it is only a statue on a summer night.

choices.text: Sit beside it on the plinth till dawn, two guards facing south

effects.log: You sit beside it all night, facing the mountain it was set to watch. It occurs to you near dawn that you and it want the same thing: a city that does not burn. The gate guards find a red feather on the plinth and argue about it all day.

choices.text: Breathe on it, to see whether it really eats fire

effects.log: You breathe a little fire onto the stone mouth. It goes in, and does not come out, and the stone does not even warm. You fly off much faster than you came, singed on the inside by your own embarrassment. A tassel on the gate catches as you go. (Ash +1)

events.text: A fire in the palace, in the queen's kitchens, in the dry season. You see it from your ridge and come north at once, and arrive over the gate in time to see that the fire has already gone out. The cooks are standing in the yard in their aprons, staring at a scorch mark that stops dead in a straight line, as if something had bitten the fire off. At the gate the stone fire-eater sits facing south. It looks well fed.
events.arc: The Stone at the Palace Gate

choices.text: Bow to the gate as you pass over

effects.log: A bow to a statue from a bird of fire, over a palace that does not see it. Somewhere in the stone, you are fairly sure, something is pleased with itself.

choices.text: Land in the kitchen yard and warm the shaking cooks

effects.log: The cooks were frightened of fire a moment ago. Now there is a red bird in the yard and they are all standing round it holding out their hands. People are very strange about fire.

events.text: An old capital at the end of its dynasty, and something walking its streets that eats iron. Needles first, the women say, then scissors, hinges, nails out of doors, the plough-shares in the fields, the swords off the soldiers sent against it. It has the bulk of a bear and is still growing. Arrows go into it and are eaten. The court is asking for a fire.
events.arc: The One Your Fire Cannot Kill

choices.text: Go and look at it before you decide anything

effects.log: From a roof you watch it eat a cart's iron tyre like a child eating a rice cake, slowly, with great content. It does not look cruel. It looks hungry, and very old, and very young at once. You fly home thinking.

choices.text: Go and burn it. A capital is asking

effects.log: You go at it out of the evening sun with everything you have. The fire runs off it like water off a duck, and it turns, quite slowly, and looks at you, and eats a gate-hinge. Then it walks off down the street with your fire still on its back, glowing. That is not good.

choices.text: Ask the swallows what the people tell their children about it

effects.log: The swallows have heard two stories under two sets of eaves. Under one, the beast cannot be killed, not even by fire. Under the other, only fire can kill it. The same name, read two ways, they say. They want to know which one is true. So do you.

events.text: The beast has gone through a quarter of the city, and the quarter is burning: forges kicked over, braziers eaten off their stands, fire running from roof to roof. And you remember both stories: the one that says fire cannot kill it, and the one that says nothing else can. A story is a fire too. You have to choose which one to feed.
events.arc: The One Your Fire Cannot Kill

choices.text: Choose the story where fire cannot kill it: put out the quarter and let it walk

effects.log: You call the fire off the streets, all of it, into yourself, and put out the burning quarter street by street. It watches you do it. Then it walks out of the city gate eating the gate's bolts, and nobody ever sees it in that capital again. (-8 health)

choices.text: Choose the story where only fire can kill it, and burn hotter than you have ever burned

ok.log: Kiln heat, then more than kiln heat, until the iron in it begins to glow and soften and run. It does not die. It melts down to something the size of a dog and walks out of the city very slowly, eating nothing. The quarter burns behind you while you do it. (Ash +1)

fail.log: It eats your heat the way it ate the arrows, and gets bigger, and the quarter burns down around the pair of you. You leave it eating a temple bell. (Ash +2, -20 health)

choices.text: Choose neither: let the monks who made it tell it to stop

effects.log: You find the old monk in a mountain hermitage who first made a little figure of rice and fed it a needle. He comes down to the city with you, very slowly, and stands in front of it and says its name the third way, the way nobody else knew, and it sits down in the road like a tired dog.

events.text: The capital falls anyway, within a few years, the way capitals do at the ends of dynasties; the beast had nothing to do with it, or everything. In the new kingdom, the story of the iron-eater is told by grandmothers, and you hear it under the eaves. In it there is a red bird. What the bird did depends on which grandmother.
events.arc: The One Your Fire Cannot Kill

choices.text: Listen to every version you can find

effects.log: In some you killed it. In some you failed. In one you are its mother. In one you married it, which you find very funny. Not one of them is right. All of them are about fire.

choices.text: Correct one grandmother, gently, from a ridge-pole

effects.log: She listens to the red bird on her roof explain what really happened, and says, "Yes, dear," and tells it her way to the children anyway. That is how stories survive.

events.text: A village smith in the south asks you, one evening, why his forge has gone quiet. Every nail he makes this year goes missing in the night. You follow the trail of missing nails up into the hills and find, in a cave, something the size of a dog, shaggy, iron-bristled, curled up asleep on a heap of them. It is very small now. It is breathing.
events.arc: The One Your Fire Cannot Kill

choices.text: Leave it a pile of nails a year, from your own smith's forge

effects.log: One basket of nails every autumn, left at the cave mouth. The smith grumbles and makes them. The thing in the cave eats them and stays small and goes nowhere, and nothing in that valley is ever eaten that should not be.

choices.text: Warm the cave, once, and go

effects.log: One warm night for a thing your fire could not kill. It does not wake. You hope it dreams of something better than iron.

events.text: You land on a palace roof to rest, one summer, and by evening the whole court is out looking at you. By the next morning there is a proclamation. A divine bird has come down, it says, as divine birds do only in the reign of a virtuous king. The king is very pleased. A branch of a tall, broad-leaved tree has been set in a bronze stand on the terrace for you to perch on, with bamboo seed and spring water.

choices.text: Eat the bamboo seed. It is free food

effects.log: You eat the whole dish, which you are fairly sure the other bird would not have done so fast, and drink the water, and fly off. The court writes it up as a great omen. The king's reign is neither better nor worse for it.

choices.text: Leave at once. You are not who they think, and it matters

effects.log: You go before dawn. A good king would not need you. A bad one should not have you. The proclamation is read out in every county anyway, with a description of you that is wrong in every particular.

choices.text: Perch on the branch, to be polite

effects.log: You perch on it, to be polite, and it catches, because you are fire and it is a branch. It burns very beautifully in its bronze stand, in front of the whole court, while you sit in the middle of it. The proclamation is not withdrawn, but it goes quiet. (Ash +1)

events.text: On the observatory roof at night: {npc}, the old court astronomer, who has kept the records of the sky for forty years and has an opinion about the proclamation. "You are the bird of the south," {he} says to the dark, without turning round. "One bird. Fire, summer, the seven mansions. The other bird is a pair, and perches on the parasol tree, and is the one kings like. I have to write the record. What shall I write?"

choices.text: "Write the truth. The other bird is the one kings like"

mem.note: told me to write the truth

effects.log: {npc} writes it, in a small clear hand at the bottom of the day's record, where the king will never read it: a bird of the south was seen; it was not the other bird. Centuries later a historian finds the line and laughs out loud in the archive.

choices.text: "Write whatever keeps you out of trouble"

mem.note: told me to keep my head

effects.log: "I am sixty-eight," {npc} says. "There is very little trouble left that I could get into." {He} writes the truth anyway, and survives it, because nobody reads the astronomer's record.

choices.text: "Write that the south laughed"

effects.log: You laugh, on the observatory roof, and the brass sighting-tube goes red-hot and {npc} has to drop it. {He} writes, carefully: the bird of the south laughed. (Ash +1)

mem.note: laughed and burned my instrument

events.text: Decades on, another king, another proclamation, another branch on the terrace. A red bird has been seen. This time it is not you: it is a pheasant that a courtier has dyed with safflower and let loose in the garden, and it is sitting in the bronze stand looking very unhappy, and the court is bowing to it.

choices.text: Land beside it, so the court can compare

effects.log: You land on the terrace beside the dyed pheasant. The court looks from one to the other. The pheasant takes one look at you and runs for the kitchens, dropping safflower. The courtier who dyed it resigns that afternoon.

choices.text: Leave it. The pheasant is doing very well, and it is not your reign

effects.log: The pheasant is fed bamboo seed for the rest of its long, nervous life, and the reign is the reign. You think of the astronomers on their observatory roofs, who would have enjoyed this enormously, and wish you could tell somebody.

choices.text: Free the pheasant: carry it off the terrace and drop it in a rice field

effects.log: The pheasant lands in the paddy and stands there, pink and wet, astonished to be nobody's omen any more. You feel exactly the same way about yourself.

events.text: Dusk on the southern coast, and the sea is full of sails: not a raid, not forty boats, but a fleet, with horses on the decks. On the beacon hill above the bay the soldiers stand looking at it with their torches in their hands. For generations they have lit one fire each evening, for peace. The captain turns to the chimneys, and to you on the nearest one, and says very quietly, "Five."

choices.text: Light all five yourself, at once, so no one's hand shakes

effects.log: Five chimneys, one breath. The fires go up together, tall and straight in the still evening, and on the next hill to the north, faint, a soldier sees them and turns to his own chimneys. The road has begun.

choices.text: Let the soldiers light them. It is their hill and their duty

effects.log: One fire, then two, then three, four, five, with the captain counting aloud and the soldiers' hands shaking. You only steady the fifth when the wind gets at it. They did it. They will remember they did it.

choices.text: Make sure first: fly out over the fleet and count it

ok.log: Over the masts in the last light: three hundred ships, horses, siege timber. You are back on the chimney before the captain has finished saying your name. "Five," you say. The fires go up.

fail.log: The archers on the lead ships have been waiting all day for something to shoot. You come back with arrows in your tail and a count that is good enough. Five. (-15 health)

events.text: You fly the beacon road north ahead of the fire, hill to hill, to see that every post answers. Most do: five fires springing up on each hill a breath after the last. Then a hill where nothing happens. Fog has come up out of a valley and wrapped the post, and the soldiers on it cannot see the fires to the south. The road stops there.

choices.text: Burn the fog off the hill with your own heat

effects.log: You circle the hill burning until the fog thins and lifts, and the soldiers see five fires to the south at last and scramble for their torches. The road runs on. You are very tired. There are a great many hills still. (-8 health)

choices.text: Land on the post and light its five yourself

effects.log: The soldiers in the fog hear wings, and then see five fires go up on their own chimneys without a hand on them, and fall flat on the ground. The road runs on. One of them will be a monk within the year.

choices.text: The captain's line keeps this post. Wake them and trust them

effects.log: It is the family of the soldier who once lit two fires in the rain for what they truly saw. The post is held by a great-grandchild now, who wakes at your voice and, without asking a single question, lights five by touch in the fog. The road runs on.

choices.text: Run the message on foot, the old way, as the law says in fog

effects.log: A runner to the next hill, by law, when the fire cannot be seen. You carry the runner, which is not in the law, and the runner shouts the message from your back over the next post, and the road runs on.

events.text: The southern hill of the capital, before dawn. Five fires on it, the last of the road, and in the palace below the secretaries are running with lamps to wake the king. You sit on the fifth chimney, scorched and empty. The whole south is lit behind you in a line of fives, all the way to the sea.

choices.text: Stay on the chimney until the army marches out

effects.log: At first light the gates open and the army goes out south under the five fires, and every soldier looks up at the red bird on the chimney. You do not move until the last of them is out of the gate.

choices.text: Fly straight back down the road to the coast, ahead of the army

effects.log: Back down the whole road without resting, to be over the bay when the landing comes. You arrive half dead. The fleet has not landed yet. It is waiting for something. You think it saw the fires too. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go down to the palace and tell the king what you saw

effects.log: A red bird on the sill of the council hall at dawn, reporting three hundred ships and horses on the decks to a king in his sleeping robe. The secretaries write it down with shaking brushes. The army marches knowing what it will find.

events.text: The landing comes at the next dawn, and the coast is ready for it because of a night of fire. On the bay below the beacon hill, the soldiers who light it every evening are holding the beach with their backs to their hill. The fire on the hill behind them is the only thing they have that the enemy does not.

choices.text: Pour your fire into your Beacon until the whole hill blazes like a wall

effects.log: The beacon hill goes up like a second sunrise behind the soldiers, and the enemy on the beach sees a mountain on fire and a red bird in it, and the landing breaks. Your Beacon has burned a lifetime in one morning. It will be fierce before long. (The Beacon aged 15 years.)

choices.text: Drop on the boats still coming in, one by one, and turn them back

ok.log: Boat after boat sees you coming and turns for the ships. By noon the landing is a few hundred men on a beach with nothing behind them, and they throw down their arms.

fail.deathCause: arrows over a beach on the night after all five beacons burned
fail.log: There are too many boats and too many archers. You turn back a third of them and come down on the beach yourself with arrows in both wings. The soldiers drag you up the hill. (-20 health)

choices.text: Keep above the soldiers on the beach, warm and bright, so they stand

effects.log: You hang over the beach all day, and the soldiers fight under you without once looking up, and do not break. It is the hardest thing you have ever done: to burn and not strike.

events.text: Autumn. The fleet has gone home. On every beacon hill from the coast to the capital the soldiers light one fire at dusk again, for peace, and you fly the road once more to see it: one fire, one fire, one fire, all the way north. On the hill above the bay there are new graves under the chimneys.

choices.text: Sit at the graves at dusk, when the one fire is lit

effects.log: The soldiers light the one fire and see you sitting among the graves and say nothing. They leave a bowl of rice for you, as for the dead. You eat it. It is the south's way.

choices.text: Teach the youngest soldier on each hill to read the sea, as you do

effects.log: One soldier a hill, all down the road: how sails sit when they carry horses, how smoke lies before fog. It takes the winter. For a long time after, the southern beacon road has the best eyes in the kingdom.

choices.text: Sing the five fires once more, from the southern hill, so it is remembered

effects.log: The night all five burned, hill by hill, sung from the capital's southern hill. The city stops to listen. Every child in it can sing the beacon road by spring.

events.text: The keeper of your Hearth is old now. {npc} has fed the fire jar every night for longer than anyone in the house can remember, and has outlived most of {his} own generation. This morning {he} kneels at the jar as always and blows, and it takes a long time to get up again. A child is watching from the door, yawning.

choices.text: Burn up bright as {he} blows, so the child sees how it is done

effects.log: The ember flares red under {npc}'s breath, the way it did when it was first lit. The child stops yawning. That night the child asks to blow on the jar, and {npc} lets the child do it, and watches, and does not help.

choices.text: Keep the jar warm all night so {he} need not kneel in the morning

effects.log: The jar is warm every morning now, already lit. {npc} kneels anyway. Some things are not about the fire.

choices.text: Show yourself in the jar, the way you did on the coldest night

effects.log: A red point in the ash that blinks. {npc} sits back on {his} heels and laughs, an old person's laugh, and says to the jar, "I knew it was you. I always knew." The child thinks the old one has gone soft in the head.

choices.text: Leave it be. A fire that is kept does not need its giver watching

effects.log: You go on along your circuit. When you come back in a year, {npc} is still kneeling at the jar every morning, and the child is kneeling beside {him}.

events.text: The potter who keeps your Kiln is the fourth of a line. {npc} fires the kiln the way the first one did, forty hours of pine, but {his} hands shake now, and {his} own children have gone into the salt trade. There is an apprentice, a sullen one, who sits by the firebox at night and talks to the fire in a voice {he} thinks nobody hears.

choices.text: Answer the apprentice, very quietly, from the firebox

effects.log: The apprentice nearly drops the stoking pole. Then sits down again, closer. By the next firing the apprentice is not sullen, only quiet, and the jade-green comes out of that kiln as true as ever. {npc} notices, and does not ask.

choices.text: Burn your truest for the old potter's last great firing

effects.log: Forty hours at your hottest and steadiest. When the kiln is opened, every piece in it has the kingfisher colour, and {npc} sits on the kiln step holding a bowl in {his} shaking hands for the whole of the afternoon.

choices.text: Let the fire go cool and see whether the line wants it

effects.log: The next firing comes out brown. The apprentice is the one who climbs into the cold firebox in the night and blows. You come up out of the ash at the third breath. The line wants it.

events.text: On the beacon hill where your Beacon burns, the keeper of it, {npc}, is the fifth of {his} family to light the one fire at dusk. {He} has never seen a raid. {His} grandfather saw three. Tonight {he} lights the fire, sits beside it, and says to it, quite clearly, "Nothing ever happens. Is this all a life is for?"

choices.text: Burn a little brighter, so {he} knows a fire for nothing is still a fire

effects.log: The one fire burns a little brighter for the rest of the evening. {npc} watches it for a long time, and then says, "Yes. All right." Nothing happens for the rest of {his} life, which is what a beacon is for.

choices.text: Tell {him} about the night all five burned

effects.log: From the next chimney, in the dark, you tell the whole night, hill by hill. {npc} listens without moving. At the end {he} only says, "I hope I never see it." Then, after a while, "I hope I would light it."

choices.text: Flare up, and frighten {him} for the fun of it

effects.log: The beacon fire goes up a man's height at once and {npc} falls off the platform into the gorse. {He} climbs back up swearing, and then laughs until {he} has to sit down. The gorse smoulders all night. (Ash +1)

events.text: Word on the wind, from a swallow: a keeper of yours has died, and nobody in the house will take the fire on. It is burning lower every month, in a house that has stopped feeding it.

choices.text: Find a new keeper for the Hearth: the neighbour's youngest, who always comes to warm up

effects.log: The neighbour's youngest has been sneaking in to warm up at that hearth for years. You sit in the jar and let the child find you blinking. The child carries the fire jar home under a coat. The Hearth burns on in a new house.

choices.text: Find a new keeper for the Field Fire: a widow with a burnt slope and no help

effects.log: You light the slope again for the widow, and stay a season to keep the wind off it. The millet comes up. The Field Fire has a keeper who needs it.

choices.text: Find a new keeper for the Lantern: the ferry's new hand, who is afraid of the dark

effects.log: The new ferry hand has been poling in the dark and praying. One night the lantern on the pole lights itself. The hand bows to it and never prays again, and never misses a night of keeping it either.

choices.text: Let the house decide. A fire nobody wants should be let go gently

effects.log: You do nothing. Perhaps someone in the house will take it on in the end. Perhaps it will go out, quietly, with no harm in it. Either way, it was theirs to decide.

events.text: A swallow again, and the same news from another eave: a keeper is dead, no heir, and the fire is guttering in a place nobody tends any more.

choices.text: Find the Kiln a keeper: the old potter's sullen apprentice

effects.log: You go into the cold firebox and wait. The apprentice comes in the night, as you knew the apprentice would. The Kiln has a keeper again, and the kingfisher colour a little longer in the world.

choices.text: Find the Beacon a keeper: a soldier's widow who climbs the hill every dusk anyway

effects.log: She has been climbing the hill at dusk since the burial to light the one fire, though nobody asked her to and the army does not pay her. You make sure it lights every time. The army, in the end, puts her on the roll.

choices.text: Find the Rite Candle a keeper: the lineage's youngest, who is bored at the rites
