effects.log: You flicker at the bored child during the rite until the child stops being bored, and looks, and is caught. Many years later the same child, grey now, still lights the candle at every rite and tells the young ones to watch it.

choices.text: Let it go. It burned long enough, and someone else's fire will warm that house

effects.log: You let it gutter. It goes out in the spring with no harm in it. You will light another somewhere else. That is what a giver of fire does.

events.text: The clerk who kept your Lamp of the Court has died at the desk, and the office has been given to a new man who uses a cheap oil lamp and keeps your fire in a cupboard. It burns lower every month. In the cupboard, among the old files, nobody can read by it.

choices.text: Find it a keeper: the junior copyist who stays after dark

effects.log: The junior copyist stays after dark every night to finish other people's work. You let the cupboard door swing open. The copyist takes the lamp out, sets it on the desk, and reads by it for years. Every forged deed in that county blackens in its light.

choices.text: Leave it in the cupboard. Courts get the light they deserve

effects.log: It goes out among the files that winter, without harm. The county's deeds are read by cheap oil for a generation, and a great many of them are forged. You told yourself it was not your court.

events.text: The keeper of your Field Fire has a grown child with a grudge: the family on the next slope moved a boundary stone in the spring. A swallow comes to you in a hurry. In the night the child took a brand from your fire, carried it across the ridge and laid it in the neighbours' dry millet. Your fire is running up the wrong slope.

choices.text: Go at once and call the brand home off the neighbours' slope

effects.log: You get there as it reaches the terraces and pull it back off them, a line of fire coming home to you up the hill. Half a field is lost. Nobody is hurt. Your own fire, on its own slope, now has a keeper's child who knows how to use it. (-6 health)

choices.text: Burn a firebreak across the ridge, quickly, and let what is lit burn out

ok.log: A clean black line across the ridge in an hour. The neighbours' millet burns to it and stops. A field lost, a slope saved. It is still fire you made. (Ash +1)

fail.log: The wind changes while you are burning the break, and the break becomes a second fire. By dawn the neighbours have lost their terraces and their barn. (Ash +2)

choices.text: Let the slope burn and go and find the child

effects.log: You let the neighbours' slope burn and go hunting through the hills for the child, and find the child at dawn in a cave, crying. Behind you a whole family's year of millet is ash, and so is a little of you. (Ash +2)

events.text: The keeper, {npc}, knows what the child did. {He} is sitting by your Field Fire on the home slope in the dark, with {his} hands over {his} face, and the child is gone into the hills. {He} looks up when your heat reaches {him}, and does not try to explain.

choices.text: Call the fire home. A fire that has been used for harm cannot stay

effects.log: You take the Field Fire back into your breast in front of {npc}, coal by coal, and the home slope goes dark. {He} does not say a word. In the spring {his} family burns the slope with ordinary fire, badly, and the millet is thin, and {he} never forgives you.

mem.note: took our fire back

choices.text: Forgive: sit by the fire with {him} until the child comes home

effects.log: Three nights. On the fourth the child comes down out of the hills, filthy and frightened, and sees the red bird by the fire and kneels. You do not say anything. {npc} does. In the spring the child carries millet to the neighbours for a whole year, and the fire warms again.

mem.note: sat with me and forgave my child

choices.text: Punish: burn the boundary stone the child fought over to powder

effects.log: The stone cracks in your heat and falls to grit, and the boundary with it. Neither family can say where the line was. {npc} stares at you. The child does not come home. (Ash +1)

events.text: The burnt terraces on the neighbours' slope, the next spring. The family that moved the boundary stone has lost its millet and its seed, and is sitting in the black field arguing about whether to leave the mountain.

choices.text: Warm their seed-bed so the late millet comes up in time

effects.log: A whole spring of warm nights over their seed-bed. The late millet comes up thick in the ash, as millet does after fire. They stay. They put the boundary stone back where it was before they moved it, and say nothing about it.

choices.text: Leave them. They moved the stone first

effects.log: They leave the mountain in the autumn. The slope goes back to scrub. The child who burned it grows up with a story in which the red bird took their side. You did not. You did nothing, which is a side.

events.text: Long years on. The keeper's child is grown, with children, and keeps your Field Fire now, and burns the home slope every spring as carefully as anyone ever has, and leaves a bowl of millet on the boundary stone every autumn for the neighbours, who leave one back. Tonight the child, who is not a child, looks up at the ridge where you sit.

choices.text: Come down and sit by the fire, once

effects.log: You sit by the field fire at the edge of the burn with the keeper's child who is not a child. Neither of you mentions the night. You do not need to. The fire burns very clean.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge. Some things are mended best without the one who saw them

effects.log: You stay on the ridge. Below, the keeper bows to it, and goes on with the burn. That is all either of you needed.

events.text: The fire you gave to the kiln has been carried to a forge in the hills: its keeper has taken a smith's work, and your fire with it. A swallow comes to you from the hills with a cold report. The smith's forge is working day and night, and it is not making ploughs. A lord of the south has gathered swordsmen and means to take the throne, and his blades are being forged in your fire.

choices.text: Go and see for yourself

effects.log: You come down on the forge chimney at night. Rows of blades on the racks. Soldiers in dark armour at the door. The smith at the anvil, working in your fire as if it were any fire. The swallow was right.

choices.text: Trust the swallow. Think before you act

effects.log: You do not go yet. You sit on your ridge with it, a hot coal of a thought, the whole night. Your fire is in the usurper's forge. Whatever you do now, you will have done it to the south.

events.text: The forge, at night, and {npc}, your keeper, at the anvil, alone for once: the soldiers are drinking in the yard. {He} sees you on the chimney and freezes with the hammer up. "They will kill my family if I stop," {he} says, before you have said anything. "Do what you came to do."

choices.text: Call the fire home. Let the forge go cold

effects.log: You draw the fire up out of the forge into your breast in a stream of sparks, and the forge is only stone. The lord's men find a cold forge and a red feather. They take it out on {npc}, but {he} lives, and makes no more swords. The Kiln is lost.

mem.note: took the fire and the lord took it out on me

choices.text: Make the swords brittle: sit in the forge and burn the temper out of every blade

ok.log: Night after night, a little too hot, at the very moment of the quench. {npc} feels it in the hammer and says nothing. The blades ring true and look perfect and will break at the first hard blow. The lord is very pleased with them.

mem.note: spoiled the swords and saved my family

fail.log: Too hot, too long. A whole rack of blades warps on the bench, and the soldiers see it, and {npc} is beaten for it, and you have to flee with a spear-graze down your side. The forge goes on. (Ash +1, -8 health)

choices.text: Let it be. Thrones are not the business of fire

effects.log: You leave. The forge goes on in your fire, which burns faster and older now with the work it is doing. Somewhere in the south, a war is being made out of a gift you gave a potter.

events.text: The lord's swordsmen march on the capital in the spring, and meet the royal guard at a river crossing. You watch from a pine. At the first clash a hundred blades break at once, ringing like bells, and the lord's army stands in the shallows holding hilts.

choices.text: Stay silent. Men are dying in the shallows either way

effects.log: Not many: an army without swords surrenders fast. But some. You watch every one of them, because you made the swords that broke, and the breaking was a kind of fire too.

choices.text: Laugh. You cannot help it

effects.log: You laugh, and the pine you are sitting in catches, and every soldier on both sides looks up at a red bird in a burning tree laughing at them. The lord's army surrenders. Some of it is the laugh. (Ash +1)

events.text: The lord has worked out who spoiled the swords, or who called his forge cold. A swordmaster in his service, a patient one, has been following the red bird's circuit for a season, and tonight steps out onto the ridge where you roost with a blade quenched in the cold spring under the White Tiger's mountain, and a net over one shoulder.

choices.text: Fight

ok.log: Cold steel against fire, on a ridge at midnight. The blade is very good, and you are better. The swordmaster ends on the ground with a melted net and a scorched sleeve, and walks home, and does not come back.

fail.deathCause: a blade quenched in cold water, on a ridge at midnight
fail.log: The cold blade cuts through your fire to the feather, and the net is on you before you can rise. You burn out of it with the last of your heat and fall off the ridge into the dark. (-25 health)

choices.text: Fly. A sword cannot follow the summer wind

effects.log: Up into the hot wind off the sea, and the swordmaster is a small figure on a ridge with a net, getting smaller. A fire does not have to win every fight. It only has to keep burning.

choices.text: Speak to the swordmaster: the lord has fallen; whose quarrel is this now?

effects.log: A long silence on the ridge. Then the swordmaster sheathes the cold blade and sits down on a rock and laughs, tiredly. "Nobody's," comes the answer. "Nobody's at all." You watch the dawn come up together, and then the swordmaster goes home.

events.text: The keeper of your Lantern now is {npc}, who poles the ferry at night when nobody else will, and talks to the lantern. Not the way the old ferry-keepers did, about fares and weather: {npc} tells it about the stars, and the river, and a song {he} cannot get the second verse of, and waits for answers. You have started listening for {his} voice when you fly the circuit.

choices.text: Flicker the answers

effects.log: {npc} notices on the second night. By the tenth, the two of you have a language: one flicker yes, two no, a long glow for I do not know either. {He} laughs at the long glows. You find yourself saving them up.

choices.text: Sing the second verse of the song, very low, from inside the lantern

effects.log: The second verse, the right one, sung by a lantern on a ferry pole. {npc} sits very still until it is finished and then says, "Again." You sing it again. You sing it most nights for a year.

choices.text: Burn steady and say nothing. A keeper is not a friend

effects.log: You burn perfectly steady. {npc} talks anyway, every night, and does not seem to need an answer. That is harder to listen to than you expected.

events.text: A summer evening on the landing. {npc} is waiting for the last passengers and they have not come. You do something you have never done: you come out of the lantern and stand at the top of the bank as a stranger, in a long red robe, with your crest folded into your hair. {npc} looks up. "You are late," {he} says, "for the last crossing. I will take you anyway."

choices.text: Cross the river with {him}, and talk the whole way

mem.note: crossed with me at dusk in a red robe

effects.log: The river is wide and you make it wider, asking about the stars. On the far bank you get off and walk away into the dark, and {npc} calls after you, "Tomorrow? The same time?" You do not answer. You are there the next evening.

choices.text: Ask {him} the second verse of the song, as if you did not know it

mem.note: knew my song

effects.log: {npc} sings it, badly, and stops, and stares at you, because you have hummed the rest without meaning to. Neither of you says anything about it. The lantern on the pole, behind you both, is empty and still burning.

choices.text: Turn and go back up the bank before {he} can see your face

effects.log: You go. {npc} stands with the pole in both hands, looking at the empty bank, and then at the lantern, and then at the bank again. That night {he} does not talk to the lantern at all.

events.text: A whole summer of evenings: the last crossing, a stranger in red, the river. {npc} has stopped asking where you go after, and started bringing two rice balls instead of one. On the night of the lantern festival the whole river is lit, and {he} looks from the ten thousand lanterns to the one on the ferry pole, and from that to you.

choices.text: Tell {him} what you are

mem.note: were the lantern all along

effects.log: "I know," {npc} says. "Since the second verse." {He} hands you the second rice ball. You sit on the landing among ten thousand lanterns and eat it, and your robe smokes a little at the hem, and neither of you minds.

choices.text: Keep it a secret. Let the summer be only a summer

effects.log: You say nothing, and {npc} asks nothing, and the summer is only a summer, and it is the best one either of you will have. In the autumn the stranger in red stops coming, and the lantern burns on.

choices.text: Leave before the festival ends. You do not grow old, and {he} will

effects.log: You walk up the bank in the middle of the festival and do not come down again as a stranger. The lantern on the ferry pole burns all night. {npc} sits under it and does not ask it anything. What you feel you swallow, and it sits beside the rest.

events.text: Decades. {npc} is grey and poles the ferry slowly, and a grandchild does the night crossings now. You have not changed at all. When you come down the bank in red at dusk, {he} looks at you for a long time, and then laughs, and says, "It is very rude of you, staying the same."

choices.text: Sit on the landing with {him} through the evening, as before

effects.log: The rice balls, the river, the lantern. {He} talks about the grandchild's poling and the stars. Nothing about you is different, and everything about {him} is, and it is still the same evening.

choices.text: Come as an old stranger, to keep {him} company in it

effects.log: You make your borrowed face old for the evening, grey and lined. {npc} studies it and shakes {his} head. "No," {he} says. "That is worse. Come as you are." You do, after that.

choices.text: Stay in the lantern now. A stranger who does not age frightens a village

effects.log: You do not come down the bank again. {npc} talks to the lantern every night, as at the start. You flicker. It is not the same, and it is enough.

events.text: {npc} is dying in the hut on the bank, and has had the grandchild bring the ferry lantern in and hang it from the rafter over the bed. It is the only light in the room. {He} looks up at it and says, without any fear in it, "Will you go out with me? Or will you stay with the child?"

choices.text: Stay with the child. Burn on for the next keeper

effects.log: You burn all night over the bed, low and warm, and near dawn {npc} says, "Good. The child is afraid of the dark," and stops. In the morning the grandchild takes the lantern down from the rafter and carries it out to the ferry pole. You burn there for many years more.
effects.npcPass: old age, under the ferry lantern

choices.text: Go out with {him}. Some fires should end with their keepers

effects.log: You burn until {npc} stops breathing, and then you let yourself go out, gently, all at once, the way a lantern does when someone blows it. The grandchild finds a cold lantern and the old keeper smiling at it. The Lantern is gone. You do not regret it.
effects.npcPass: old age, as the lantern went out

choices.text: Come down as the stranger in red, one last time, and sit by the bed

effects.npcPass: old age, holding a stranger's hand
effects.log: The grandchild comes in at dawn to find a stranger in a red robe sitting by the bed, and the old keeper gone, smiling. The stranger stands, bows to the grandchild very low, and walks out. The lantern on the rafter is still burning.

events.text: A drought year. No rain since the barley, and the rice paddies cracking into plates, and the wells going down a hand a week. You have known for a month that half of it is you: you are hot, and you are summer, and summer is sitting on the south and will not get up. The other half is that the rain is somewhere else.

choices.text: Bank yourself down: go and sit in the coldest cave you can find

effects.log: A month in a cave behind a waterfall, banked so low you can barely move. The south is a little cooler for it. The rain still does not come. You come out grey at the edges. (-8 health)

choices.text: Keep burning. Summer is summer; the rain is not your affair

effects.log: You burn, because you are what you are. The paddies crack further. In the villages they start to look at the red bird on the ridge the way you would look at a wolf. (The summer you held is counted.)

choices.text: Find out where the rain is

effects.log: The swallows know. The rain is standing over the next province east, piled up in great black towers over one valley, held there. Somebody is keeping it.

events.text: The border of two provinces: on your side, white sky and cracked earth; on the other, a valley so green it hurts, under clouds that sit on the eastern hills like a lid. The Azure Dragon is keeping its valley's rain, and its valley is drinking. You fly to the edge of the clouds, where heat meets wet, and the air shudders.

choices.text: Ask for half the rain for your province, politely, at the edge of the storm

ok.log: Thunder, a long way in, considering. Then the edge of the clouds moves, slowly, west, over the border, and the first drops hiss on your feathers. Your province gets three days of rain. You did not even have to sing.

fail.log: The clouds do not move. A voice in the thunder says the valley planted late and needs it more. Perhaps it does. You go home to your cracked paddies and sit with that.

choices.text: Go and sit on the eastern hills and cool yourself on the Dragon's clouds

effects.log: You sit in the wet at the edge of the storm for a week and stop being quite so hot. The clouds, perhaps noticing a bird that is no longer quarrelling, drift a little west. Some rain falls on your side. Not enough. Some.

choices.text: Push your heat into the storm until it breaks and spills your way

effects.log: Hot against wet, all afternoon. The storm boils and breaks and comes west in a rush, hail and wind, and flattens what is left of your province's rice, and floods two villages on the border. It rained. (Ash +1)

events.text: On the hilltop above a dry village the rain rite is in its third day. The children are beating clay jars with sticks, chanting at the dragons inside to make rain; a straw dragon has been beaten until it is mostly straw. And on a pole above the altar, there is a red bird made of paper, and the village elder {npc} is about to set it on fire. You are on the ridge-pole of the shrine.

choices.text: Speak: "Burn it. I would, in your place"

mem.note: told me to burn the paper one

effects.log: {npc} drops the torch, and picks it up, and looks at you, and burns the paper bird very respectfully. The children cheer. The rain does not come that day. It comes on the fifth, and the village says it was the bird that gave itself up.

choices.text: Speak: "You have the wrong villain. The rain is held in the east"

mem.note: said the rain was held in the east

effects.log: {npc} listens to the whole explanation with a face like stone. Then {he} says, "Can you make it come?" You cannot. "Then you are still the villain," {he} says, and burns the paper bird.

choices.text: Say nothing. Take the paper bird's place on the pole

mem.note: sat on the pole to be burned

effects.log: You land on the pole and knock the paper bird off it and sit there. {npc} lowers the torch. Nobody can bring themselves to set fire to the real thing. You sit there until the rain comes, nine days later. (-5 health)

events.text: The rains come at last, late and heavy, and you sit on your ridge with your feathers hissing and steaming and let them come. Down in the cracked paddies the farmers are standing in the downpour with their hats off. A drought is not a thing you did. It is not a thing you did not do, either.

choices.text: Think about it: a summer is a fire you share with the whole sky

effects.log: Heat and rain, east and south, fire and water. You are one of them. You are not the sky. The rain runs off your tail feathers into the paddy, and you feel smaller than you have in years, and better.

choices.text: Send one warm wind east, to dry the Dragon's flooded valley

effects.log: In the east, the valley that kept the rain has too much of it now. One warm wind from the south, for a week, and its rice stands up again. The thunder says nothing. Its rain falls on your side for the rest of the summer.

choices.text: Sulk. They made you the villain

effects.log: Villain of the drought, and now the rain comes as if nothing had happened. You sit in it and keep the thing, hot and sour, under your breastbone.

events.text: The county office, long after the magistrate has gone home. One window still lit, badly: an oil lamp guttering on a low desk, and a clerk, {npc}, reading land deeds with {his} nose almost on the paper. A widow's field is being taken on the strength of one of them. {npc} thinks it is forged and cannot prove it, and the lamp keeps going out.

choices.text: Become the clerk's lamp. Forged papers will blacken in your light

effects.log: You come in through the lattice and settle in the lamp, and it burns up clear and red and steady. {npc} looks up, and then down, and the deed on the desk is going black at the edges, slowly, from the forged seal outwards. {He} sits back. Then {he} bows to the lamp. The Lamp of the Court is lit.

choices.text: Light the lamp for one night only, and watch what {he} does

effects.log: One night of clear light. {npc} reads the deed by it and finds the forger's hand plain as day, and goes to the magistrate in the morning with it, and is shouted at, and goes again. The widow keeps the field. You think the clerk would keep a fire well.

choices.text: Leave it. A court is the one place your fire would be used against people

effects.log: You fly on. Behind you the oil lamp gutters out and {npc} sits in the dark office, holding a deed {he} cannot read.

events.text: From the office roof at night. {npc} has kept your lamp a year now, and the county has noticed: deeds blacken on that desk, and false witnesses stammer in that light. Tonight {he} comes out into the yard with the lamp in both hands and says up to the roof, "A minister's steward brought me a deed today. It blackened. If I say so, I will lose my post, and maybe more. Tell me what to do."

choices.text: "Say so. I will be on the roof when the steward comes back"

mem.note: stood by me from the roof

effects.log: {npc} says so. The steward comes back with men. The men look up at the red bird with the burning crest on the office roof and remember appointments elsewhere. The deed is struck from the register. The minister writes a letter, and the letter, on that desk, blackens too.

choices.text: "Say nothing yet. Copy the deed, and wait for an honest magistrate"

mem.note: told me to wait for the right magistrate

effects.log: Six years. {npc} keeps the copy in a sleeve and the lamp on the desk, and when the honest magistrate comes, {he} lays both on the new magistrate's desk in the same night. A minister falls. It took six years. It was the right six years.

choices.text: "A lamp shows. It does not judge. That is your work"

mem.note: said the judging was mine

effects.log: {npc} stands in the yard with the lamp for a long time. Then {he} nods and goes in. What {he} does with the deed, you do not ask. The lamp burns on the desk the next night just the same.

events.text: There is a star beside the Well in the southern sky called the Axe, and the old books say it watches for excess and cuts it off. The new magistrate of {npc}'s county has read the old books, and wants the lamp in the great hall: a lamp that shows the guilty, says the magistrate, should also burn them, and this is meant literally. {npc} has come out to the yard, pale, with the lamp.

choices.text: Refuse, through the clerk: the lamp shows; it never burns

effects.log: The lamp stays on {npc}'s desk. When the magistrate's men come to take it, it goes out in their hands and lights again on the desk the moment they set it down. After the third time they stop trying.

choices.text: Let the magistrate have it, and see whether the magistrate dares

effects.log: The lamp goes to the hall. The first accused brought before it is guilty, and the lamp flares, and a sleeve catches, and the magistrate, who wanted exactly this, is so frightened that the seal of office is handed back within the month. Nobody died. Somebody nearly did. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Burn the magistrate's copy of the old book, the page with the Axe on it

effects.log: One page, curled to ash in the night, the one about the Axe star. The magistrate reads the book again in the morning, finds nothing about burning anyone, and decides it was all misremembered. (Ash +1)

events.text: Your Lamp of the Court has burned thirty years without renewing, and it has grown fierce. {npc}'s office is full of quarrels now. Clerks shout. Witnesses weep for no reason. In that hard light even honest papers look a little guilty, and {npc} has started to see forgeries everywhere, in every hand, even in {his} own.

choices.text: Renew it with the season's wood, there on the desk

effects.log: Apricot and jujube twigs, rubbed new on the desk at midnight while {npc} watches. The light softens at once. In a week the office is quiet again, and {npc} sleeps for the first time in a month.

choices.text: Sing it calmer through the night, low

effects.log: A long low song in the office all night. The lamp settles, not new, but calmer. {npc} falls asleep at the desk with {his} head on a deed, and nobody shouts in the morning.

choices.text: Leave it. A court should be a hard place

effects.log: You leave it hard. {npc} sends an honest witness to the cells that year, sure the witness lied. The light was too strong for anyone to look honest in.

events.text: {npc} is old, and has asked to be carried to the office one last time, to the desk where the lamp burns. An apprentice copyist sits on the floor beside the desk with the brushes. {npc} looks at the lamp, and then at the apprentice, and then up at the lattice where you sit.

choices.text: Pass the lamp to the apprentice

effects.log: {npc} pushes the lamp across the desk with two fingers until it sits in front of the apprentice, and says, "It shows. It does not judge. That is your work." Then {he} is quiet for good. The apprentice keeps the lamp burning for years.
effects.npcPass: old age, at the desk, by the lamp

choices.text: Let the lamp go out with {him}. A court lamp should not outlive its keeper's judgment

effects.log: You burn until {npc} is gone, and then you go out on the desk, all at once. The apprentice lights an ordinary lamp. The county will read its deeds by ordinary light again, and that, perhaps, is fair.
effects.npcPass: old age, as the lamp went out

events.text: A scholar on a veranda, fanning, with a book on the five phases open on {his} knees. {npc} has been reading the same page for an hour: fire, summer, the south, the colour red, the virtue of rites. {He} looks up at the red bird on the ridge-pole and says, as if continuing an argument, "Why rites? Why should fire be the virtue of courtesy?"

choices.text: "Because a fire in a house has to be invited, fed and thanked, or it eats the house"

mem.note: explained to me why fire is courtesy

effects.log: {npc} writes it in the margin, then crosses out the page's own explanation. The book is copied with the margin in it for generations. Nobody knows who wrote the note.

choices.text: "Because I am the youngest at every table, and had to learn to bow first"

mem.note: told me it is always the youngest

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard the fan falls in the yard. "The bird of the south," {he} says, "the baby of the family." You bristle. Then you laugh too, and a roof tile cracks, and nobody minds.

choices.text: "Read the next page"

effects.log: {npc} turns the page. It says a great deal about water. {He} looks up at you, betrayed. You are already gone.

events.text: A young swordsman in the yard of an inn, with a new blade and an old master's letter: temper it in the fire of the south, the letter says, and it will never break. {npc} has climbed onto the inn's woodpile to be nearer the roof, and holds the sword up to you in both hands like an offering.

choices.text: Breathe on it once, at the right heat

mem.note: breathed on my sword

effects.log: One breath. The blade goes the colour of straw, then of a pigeon's neck, and {npc} plunges it into the inn's horse trough and the trough boils dry. The sword is very good. It never breaks. In a few years it is famous, and so is the horse trough.

choices.text: "A sword that never breaks makes a swordsman who never stops"

mem.note: would not temper my sword

effects.log: {npc} lowers the sword slowly and thinks about that for so long the inn-keeper comes out to see why. The sword breaks, years later, in a fight {he} would have done better to walk away from. {He} walks away from the next one.

choices.text: Test the swordsman first: "Strike at me"

mem.note: tested me and then tempered my sword

ok.log: The cut misses you by a feather, which is very good, and then you are behind {npc} on the woodpile. "Again," you say, and breathe on the blade. It is a good blade now. In a few years the swordsman is a good swordsman.

mem.note: let me cut a feather from you

fail.log: The cut takes a tail feather clean off, and {npc} catches it, and stands holding it, appalled. You laugh. You breathe on the sword for that alone. {He} keeps the feather in the scabbard. (-6 health)

events.text: A child of about ten stands in a cold kitchen doorway in the summer twilight, very serious, with an empty clay jar held against {his} chest. {npc}'s grandmother died in the spring, and the household fire went out at the funeral and nobody relit it properly. "Grandmother said the bird of the south gives fire to people who ask nicely," {he} says. "Please."

choices.text: Give the child a coal from your breast, into the jar

mem.note: gave me fire because I asked nicely

effects.log: One coal, dropped from the ridge-pole into the jar, glowing. {npc} carries it inside like a bowl of soup and the kitchen is warm by dark. It is not one of your seven. It is only a fire for a child who asked. Those are allowed too.

choices.text: Teach the child to bank a fire so it never goes out again

mem.note: taught me to bank the fire

effects.log: You light the kitchen fire and then sit on the stove shelf and show {npc} how: the ash, the depth, the pine needle at dawn. The child does it every night for years and teaches it to everyone.

events.text: A monk from a temple across the river, who has kept a lamp before the Buddha for forty years and has a question about it. {npc} stands under the ridge with {his} hands folded and asks it very simply. "I have watched the flame every night of my life. Is it the same flame, or a new one every moment?"

choices.text: "A new one every moment. That is why it has to be kept"

mem.note: said the flame is new every moment

effects.log: {npc} bows and goes home and sits with it for a year. Then {he} comes back and says, "And the bird?" You do not have an answer. {He} seems satisfied with that.

choices.text: "The same. I have been the same fire since a fire jar on the coldest night"

mem.note: said it has always been the same fire

effects.log: "Then you are very old," {npc} says, "for a moment." {He} smiles and goes back across the river. You think about that for a whole season.

choices.text: Answer by going out, and coming back, on the ridge-pole in front of {him}

mem.note: went out and came back

effects.log: You go out, completely, a grey bird-shape on the tiles, and then you are red again. {npc} stands under the eaves for a long time. Then {he} laughs, quietly, the way monks do, and goes home without asking anything else.

events.text: The court geomancer has come all the way south, with a compass board and two servants, to stand under the ridge-pole where you sit and read you a letter from the palace. {npc} reads it beautifully. It asks the bird of the fire mountain, with every courtesy, to find another mountain.

choices.text: "Ask me again with no letter, as yourself"

mem.note: asked me to speak for myself

effects.log: {npc} folds the letter away, and thinks, and says, "The city is afraid, and it has every reason, and you have done nothing to deserve it. Will you go anyway?" It is the best thing anyone at court has ever said to you. You tell {him} you will think about it, and mean it.

choices.text: Bow to the letter, as courtesy demands, and say nothing at all

mem.note: bowed to the king's letter

effects.log: {npc} reports to the palace that the bird bowed. The court spends a month arguing about what a bow means. You find the whole thing very restful.

choices.text: "Tell the palace the mountain was there first"

effects.log: You say it with your crest up, and the letter in {npc}'s hands catches at the corner. {He} puts it out against {his} sleeve with great dignity and bows. "I will tell them exactly that," {he} says. (Ash +1)

mem.note: burned the palace letter

events.text: A shaman in a red robe, dancing in a farmyard with a red fan, calling the south. The fan spins and stops and spins. {npc} is very good, and very tired, and the farm's sick child is no better. When {he} looks up and sees you on the ridge, the fan stops dead. "Oh," {he} says. "You actually came."

choices.text: "I came. Keep dancing. I will do the rest"

mem.note: came when I called

effects.log: {npc} dances, and you warm the sickroom from the roof all night, the way you warm a cold kitchen, slowly, through the tiles. The fever breaks at dawn. {npc} sits down in the yard with the fan in {his} lap and does not get up for an hour. (-4 health)

choices.text: "Most of the time I do not come. Tell them that, too"

mem.note: said it mostly does not come

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "I know," {he} says. "I tell them it is the dancing that matters." You help with the child anyway. {He} goes on dancing for the rest of {his} life, and tells everyone you do not come.

events.text: A grandmaster of the southern sword schools has heard that the Summer Bird speaks from ridge-poles, and is standing in the yard below in a white summer robe, with a sword {he} has not drawn in twenty years because nobody was worth it. "One exchange," {npc} says. "Only one. I want to know what summer is made of."

choices.text: Come down and give {him} the exchange

mem.note: crossed swords with me and let me lose well

ok.log: One exchange, in the yard, at noon. The sword is very fast, and you are summer. When it is over {npc} is sitting on the ground with the blade across {his} knees, glowing faintly, and laughing. "Heat," {he} says. "It is made of heat. I should have guessed."

mem.note: let me touch you with my sword

fail.log: The sword goes through your heat like a swallow through smoke, and you feel the cold of it along your wing. {npc} lowers the blade and bows very deeply. "Now I know," {he} says. (-15 health)

choices.text: "Summer is made of barley, and wells, and children. Go and look"

mem.note: told me to look at the barley

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time, and then sheathes the sword and walks out of the yard toward the fields. You hear, years later, that the grandmaster of the south took up farming, and is bad at it, and happy.

events.text: A swallow, then another: fevers in a house round one of your old fires. Children with hot foreheads, a grandfather who will not stop coughing, quarrels at the evening meal over nothing. The fire burns hotter than ever and warms everyone too much. It needs the season's wood.
events.arc: The Fevers Round an Old Fire

choices.text: Fly to the Hearth with the season's wood and rub it new

effects.log: Apricot and jujube in the summer, rubbed new in the old fire jar at dawn. The fevers break within the week. The family thinks it was the doctor.

choices.text: Fly to the Field Fire and burn the slope new

effects.log: You burn the old fire out of the slope and light it again from new wood, carefully, against the wind. The fever in the fire-field village goes down with it.

choices.text: Fly to the Lantern and renew it on its pole

effects.log: You rub the ferry lantern new on its pole at midnight. The ferry hands stop quarrelling about whose turn it is. Nobody on that river coughs this winter.

choices.text: Sing over the sick house all night instead, and leave the fire as it is

effects.log: You sing over the roof all night, low and slow. The fevers ease a little. The fire is still old. The swallows will be back.

events.text: The swallows again, from the coast and the kiln country: one of your fires there has grown fierce. The potters crack their pots for no reason; the beacon soldiers see sails where there are none and fight about it.
events.arc: The Fevers Round an Old Fire

choices.text: Renew the Kiln with the season's wood

effects.log: Into the firebox with an armful of new wood. The next firing comes out whole, every piece, and the potters stop shouting at the apprentices.

choices.text: Renew the Beacon on its chimney

effects.log: You rub the beacon fire new on its chimney at dusk. That night the soldiers see one fire and the sea and nothing else, and sleep in turns again.

choices.text: Leave it a season longer. You are busy

effects.log: You leave it. The swallows report the next spring: worse. A fire that is not renewed does not wait for you to be less busy.

events.text: From the shrines and the offices, through the swallows: your Rite Candle or your Lamp of the Court has grown old and fierce. At the rites the dead are restless. In the office the clerks see guilt in every face.
events.arc: The Fevers Round an Old Fire

choices.text: Renew the Rite Candle at the next rite

effects.log: At the midnight rite you come in with the incense smoke and rub the candle new. The ancestors settle like birds on a roof at dusk. The eldest of the lineage feels it, and bows longer than usual.

choices.text: Renew the Lamp of the Court on its desk

effects.log: On the clerk's desk at midnight, new wood rubbed to new flame. In the morning the office is quiet, and an honest witness is let go.

choices.text: Sing to it from the roof, to calm it for now

effects.log: A song from the roof. It helps a little, the way a song does. It is not new wood.

events.text: Three of your fires are fierce at once. The swallows come from every direction with the same news, and the south is full of fevers and quarrels and pots that crack in the kiln. You cannot be in three places. You have to choose an order, and the season is short.
events.arc: The Fevers Round an Old Fire

choices.text: Fly the whole circuit without resting, renewing as you go

ok.log: One season, the whole south, every fire rubbed new, one after the other, without sleep. You come back to your ridge so tired you sleep through the first frost. The swallows report no fevers anywhere. (-12 health)

fail.log: You get to two of them, and fall out of the sky on the way to the third, and lie in a paddy for a week. The third fire is still fierce. (-18 health)

choices.text: Ask the swallows which house has the youngest children, and go there first

effects.log: The swallows tell you. You go there first, and the second, and the third is a little worse for waiting. That is what choosing is.

choices.text: Sing all three calmer from a high ridge, all night, for a season

effects.log: A whole season of singing from the highest ridge in the south, to three fires at once. They settle a little, all of them. Not new. Calmer.

events.text: The Hearth you gave has burned sixty years unrenewed, and tonight it comes out of the fire jar. A coal on the kitchen floor, the floor mat, the screen door, the eaves. The family is asleep. The house beside it has a thatched roof and a wind is coming down the valley.

choices.text: Dive into it with the season's wood and rub it new, sixty years at once

ok.log: Into the front of it, with new wood in your claws, and you take the old fire by the throat and rub it young. It is the hardest renewal you have ever done. The Hearth burns quiet again, and it is morning, and nobody has died. (-10 health)

fail.log: Too old, too far gone. It will not be renewed. You fight it all night and lose, and by morning the Hearth you gave is gone and there is ash where there was warmth, and it is yours. (Ash +5, -15 health)

choices.text: Call it home before it reaches anyone

effects.log: You come down on it and draw it up into your breast, all of it, the whole sixty years, burning. It goes. The Hearth is lost. Nothing else is. You lie on the ridge for a day afterwards, too hot to move. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let it run. It is too strong, and you are tired

effects.log: You let it run. It goes up and over and on, and the swallows will not nest in that county for years. The Hearth is gone and the ash is yours. (Ash +5)

events.text: Sixty years on the same slope without new wood, and the Field Fire is not a farmer's fire any more. At noon it jumps the firebreak and goes up the mountain on the wind, through the pines, toward the next valley and the villages in it.

choices.text: Dive into it with the season's wood and rub it new, sixty years at once

ok.log: Into the front of it, with new wood in your claws, and you take the old fire by the throat and rub it young. It is the hardest renewal you have ever done. The Field Fire burns quiet again, and it is morning, and nobody has died. (-10 health)

fail.log: Too old, too far gone. It will not be renewed. You fight it all night and lose, and by morning the Field Fire you gave is gone and there is ash where there was warmth, and it is yours. (Ash +5, -15 health)

events.text: The Lantern on the ferry pole has burned sixty years without renewing. In a storm tonight it swings, and the paper catches, and the burning lantern drops onto the ferry's tarred deck in the middle of the river with a crossing full of people on it.

choices.text: Dive into it with the season's wood and rub it new, sixty years at once

ok.log: Into the front of it, with new wood in your claws, and you take the old fire by the throat and rub it young. It is the hardest renewal you have ever done. The Lantern burns quiet again, and it is morning, and nobody has died. (-10 health)

fail.log: Too old, too far gone. It will not be renewed. You fight it all night and lose, and by morning the Lantern you gave is gone and there is ash where there was warmth, and it is yours. (Ash +5, -15 health)

choices.text: Call it home before it reaches anyone

effects.log: You come down on it and draw it up into your breast, all of it, the whole sixty years, burning. It goes. The Lantern is lost. Nothing else is. You lie on the ridge for a day afterwards, too hot to move. (-8 health)

events.text: A summer banquet at a magistrate's pavilion by the river, and you on the pavilion roof because the lanterns are yours. A guest from the capital, a little drunk, looks up and says to the table that the famous bird of the south is smaller than a peacock and much less well dressed. The table laughs. You feel your crest stand up.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You hold your crest down with something like a fist. The table goes on laughing. It is not much of a joke. It goes down very hot.

choices.text: Sing it: a verse about a peacock at a banquet

effects.log: A verse from the roof, to a drinking tune, about a peacock from the capital who came to the south and found it too hot. The table laughs harder, at the guest now. The guest laughs too, eventually, which is the best you could hope for.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: Your crest goes up a yard and every lantern on the pavilion flares and two of them catch, and the guest's fan, and the edge of the awning. Nobody is hurt. The table is very quiet. (Ash +1)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: You try. It comes up anyway, too much has gone down before it: the roof under you smokes, and the guest's hat, and you have swallowed and let out at once, the worst of both. (Ash +1)

events.text: The dog days, and a temple abbot preaching in a courtyard below your perch about the sins of fire: greed, anger, and especially, he says, waving up at you, that one, which sits on roofs and burns the hats of honest scholars. The listeners turn and look. Some of them have hats.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You sit absolutely still through the whole sermon. Anger, it says. You keep it, hot, under your breastbone, with the rest.

choices.text: Bow to the abbot. On the whole, the abbot is right

effects.log: You bow from the roof, slowly. The abbot stops mid-sentence. After the sermon he comes and stands under the roof and bows back, and you sit together in the heat for a long time without saying anything.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: You flare, once, and the abbot's sermon scroll curls up in his hands and he has to drop it in the lotus pool. The listeners are delighted. The abbot is right about you, which is the worst of it. (Ash +1)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: You try to swallow it and it will not go: the temple bell rope above you catches, and burns, and drops, and the bell is silent for a month. (Ash +1)

events.text: A drought summer, and a county magistrate holds a rite for rain in the market square, and in front of the whole county reads out a charge against the red bird on the ridge: that it is a thief of rain, a pheasant with a fever, a plague of the south. He has a drum, and a red paper bird, and a great many people listening.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You sit on the ridge and take every word. A thief of rain. A plague. The drum. You keep all of it, and it is a great deal to keep.

choices.text: Sing it: a song about a magistrate who blamed a bird for the sky

effects.log: The song goes round the county faster than the charge did. By the time the rain comes, a month later, everyone is singing it, and the magistrate is transferred to the north at his own request.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: The paper bird on the magistrate's pole goes up first, and then the pole, and then the awning over the drum. The magistrate runs. The county watches its rain rite burn. In a drought. (Ash +2)

choices.text: It will not go down: try to swallow it anyway

effects.log: It will not go down. It comes out of you in one hot breath across the square, and the drum skin splits, and the paper bird burns, and you are still full of it after. (Ash +2)

events.text: The fifth day of the fifth month, the day the sun is strongest in the year's count, and the whole county is at the river: hair washed in iris water, wrestling in the sand ring, and a swing hung between two great pines so high that the best swingers kick the leaves at the top. It is a festival of summer. It is, in a sense, your festival.
events.arc: The Fifth of the Fifth Month

choices.text: Ride the hot wind above the swing, and lift the best swinger a little higher

effects.log: A gust of your heat at the top of each swing, and the girl on it kicks the highest bough anyone has ever reached, and shouts, and the whole riverbank shouts with her. Nobody sees a bird. Everybody sees summer.

choices.text: Keep the noon gentle, so the old people can stay to watch the wrestling

effects.log: You sit high and cool, drawing the heat off the sand, and the grandparents stay under the pines all afternoon. The champion is a ferry-keeper's nephew, and gets an ox.

choices.text: Come down and dance in the crowd, which is perhaps a mistake

ok.log: A red bird dancing in the crowd by the river. Children dance round you. Nothing catches, not one thing, all afternoon. It is the best day of your summer.

fail.log: You dance, and the joy comes up in you like a laugh, and the swing rope smoulders through at the top, and the swing comes down, slowly, onto the sand, with nobody on it. Nobody is hurt. (Ash +1)

events.text: Dano again, and the river, the swing, the iris water, the sand ring. You come every year now. The children of the county call the hottest hour of the festival "the bird's hour", and look up.
events.arc: The Fifth of the Fifth Month

choices.text: Give them the bird's hour: one long loop over the swing, bright as noon

effects.log: One loop, and the whole riverbank looks up and cheers, and you are gone again into the white sky. That is all they want. That is all you want.

choices.text: Watch from the pines. The festival does not need you to be in it

effects.log: You watch the whole day from the top of the swing pine. The swingers kick the leaves beside you. One of them sees you, and says nothing, and swings higher.

choices.text: Laugh at the wrestlers' fall, with a temper in you

effects.log: You laugh at a fall in the sand ring and the laugh comes out hot, and the judge's straw hat catches. The judge stamps it out to great applause. You fly off quickly. (Ash +1)

events.text: On a night after Dano, on the ridge above the river, you think about festivals. The fire-falling over the pond, the lanterns on the Buddha's birthday, the moon house at the first full moon, the swing at Dano. People make fire into joy, and heat into a holiday. They did it before you were a spark.
events.arc: The Fifth of the Fifth Month

choices.text: Think about it until the stars go round

effects.log: Every festival you know is fire made into a gift with nobody to thank for it. You were taught to give fire by the people you give it to. That is a strange thing to understand on a ridge at midnight, and you are glad to.

choices.text: Sing a festival song you made up, for nobody

effects.log: A new song, for nobody, about a swing and a river. A herd boy on the far bank hears the tune and whistles it home. It is a Dano song in that county now, nobody knows from where.

events.text: A swallow you do not know comes to your ridge at dawn, out of breath, with news from a far eave. One of your fires is being used for harm, and has been for some years, and nobody told you. It burns hotter and older for it.

choices.text: Ask about the Hearth

effects.log: A house that keeps your Hearth has turned it to harm: the old keeper's heir uses it to frighten the poor relations out of the house in winter. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Ask about the Field Fire

effects.log: Your Field Fire is being set on other people's slopes. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Ask about the Lantern

effects.log: The ferry lantern lures boats onto the sandbar at night, where men wait to rob them. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Ask about all of them, slowly, until you understand

effects.log: The swallow tells you all it knows, and it does not know everything. You will have to fly the Swallow Road and hear the rest under every eave.

events.text: A magpie, of all birds, lands beside you on the ridge-pole with news it clearly enjoys: one of your fires is in bad hands, and the whole valley knows it but you.

choices.text: Ask about the Kiln

effects.log: Your Kiln has been turned to forging for a band of robbers. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Ask about the Beacon

effects.log: Your Beacon's keeper lights false alarms for pay, to empty the coast for smugglers. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Thank the magpie and ask nothing. Magpies exaggerate

effects.log: The magpie is offended and leaves. It was probably exaggerating. Probably.

events.text: An old crow from a shrine roof, very solemn, who has watched one of your fires burn wrong for three winters and has decided, at last, that it is your business. It will tell you which, if you ask the right question.

choices.text: Ask about the Rite Candle

effects.log: The candle at the rites is burned to curse a rival lineage, name by name, at midnight. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Ask about the Lamp of the Court

effects.log: The lamp in the office is made to blacken honest papers for a bribe: a keeper who learned to tilt the wick. You know now. You can call it home.

choices.text: Ask the crow why it waited three winters

effects.log: "Because it was not my fire," says the crow, "and it took me three winters to decide that it was my village." You think about that all the way home.
